speechtext:
Since parliament in this session will be considering matters pertaining to the Canadian banking system in connection with the decennial revision of the Bank Act, it is appropriate that the Bank of Canada Act should also be revised at this time. The Bank of Canada Act was passed in 1934 and amended in 1936 and 1938. Since then the act has been amended in a number of ways by provisions in other statutes. As a result of these amendments and changing circumstances, a number of provisions of the act are either no longer operative or no longer appropriate. In addition, to bring the act up to date in these respects, it is proposed that certain revisions should be made.
In view of the proposed provision in the National Housing Act allowing chartered banks to make insured mortgage loans, it is proposed that the Bank of Canada should have the power to make short-term loans to banks on the pledge or hypothecation of insured mortgages held by them.
In addition, changes will be made in the limitations on the bank's holdings of government of Canada securities, in the amount of its rest or reserve fund and the provisions regarding cash reserves to be maintained by the chartered banks.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

maintopic: VITAMIN PRODUCTS
speechtext:
1.	Has the government during 1952-53 and to date, investigated potency of the vitamin products of certain manufacturers?
2.	If so, how many such (a) products; (b) manufacturers were investigated?
3.	What percentage of the products investigated were below labelled potency?
4.	What were the products, by advertised name, and who were the manufacturers of the products which were found to be below labelled potency?
5.	What action has the government taken as a result of these findings?

maintopic: VITAMIN PRODUCTS
speechtext:
1.	Yes. The potency of vitamin products on the Canadian market is under constant review.
2.	Approximately 1,500 products were examined from January 1, 1952 to January 31, 1954. These products were obtained from approximately 200 manufacturers.
3.	Particular attention was paid to the products of those companies which it was felt might have products below the labelled potency. Furthermore an effort was made to concentrate on those types of products which experience has shown may be more often below label claim. Of the 1,500 such products which were analysed approximately 300 were found to be below the labelled potency in one or more vitamins. However the fact that one-fifth of the products analysed did

Questions
not meet label claim should not be interpreted to mean that one-fifth of the vitamin products on the Canadian market do not meet label claim as the above figures apply only to those companies which were studied and not to the industry as a whole. It is known that the great bulk of vitamin products now on the market conform to labelled potency and are adequately labelled.
4.	Generally speaking vitamins are unstable compounds and precautions must be taken to ensure that the potency of the vitamin product is still satisfactory when it reaches the consumer. It has been found that practically all pharmaceutical companies have had on the market at some time a product which did not meet label claim for at least one vitamin. During the period January 1, 1952 to the present not all products nor all companies have been examined, hence it would be unfair to reveal the identity of those companies whose products happened to be analysed and were found to be below labelled potency in that period. Furthermore, most products which were found to be below labelled potency have subsequently been corrected or withdrawn from the market by the company. Thus it would not be desirable to name a product which was below claim two years ago but has subsequently been found to meet label claim. The survey of the vitamin
products produced in Canada is still not complete. Therefore it would be grossly discriminatory to release the findings at this time.
5.	The first approach to a manufacturer whose product has been found to be below the labelled potency has been educational. Experience has clearly shown that those companies who have adequate control facilities and who analyse their products before placing them on the market, usually have products which meet label claim. Advice is given to the manufacturer when requested regarding possible causes of the low vitamin content of the product and the institution of proper control measures. If a manufacturer persists in placing on the market a product which does not meet label claim he is given a final warning and if necessary prosecuted. If seriously below labelled potency, existing stocks of the product may be seized by the crown. Goods under seizure are forfeited to the crown and disposed of, either by reprocessing under supervision, if considered feasible, or by destruction on the order of the minister.

If there is no such committee or organization, are any steps taken to ensure that there is such co-ordination, particularly in connection with placement of immigrants, land settlement and agricultural worker schemes, and generally to ensure that the population requirements of the nation and the rights and responsibilities of the provinces are kept in harmony?

(a) Continuous liaison on departmental level is maintained between federal officials of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration and officials of provincial government departments concerned on all problems of mutual interest affecting the placement of immigrants, land settlement as it pertains to immigrants and agricultural workers schemes. Early in 1953, all provincial governments were invited to have senior departmental officials attend meetings with senior federal officers on immigration matters of mutual interest. To date, eight of the provinces have sent representatives to such meetings which were concerned principally with the development of ways and means

to achieve closer co-operation and co-ordination in the fields mentioned above. This cooperation and co-ordination is being pursued and extended wherever possible, in field activities in Canada.
(b)	As the successful establishment of immigrants is closely related to the welfare of immigrants during the early period after their arrival in Canada, the federal government, early in 1952, offered to conclude with, each of the provincial governments an agreement for the sharing on a basis of equal cost of necessary hospitalization and welfare assistance for immigrants who became indigent through accident or illness during the first year after their arrival in Canada. To date, agreements have been concluded with six of the provinces covering both hospitalization and welfare assistance, while an agreement covering hospitalization expenses only has been concluded with yet another province. The provincial governments are responsible for the operational administration of these agreements and accounts for the federal share are submitted to the federal Department of Labour.
(c)	With particular reference to agricultural workers, federal-provincial farm labour agreements have been entered' into by the federal Department of Labour with each of the provinces of Canada with the exception of Newfoundland. These agreements provide for co-operative action in relation to the recruitment, distribution and placement of farm labour. A federal-provincial farm labour committee is set up in each province and in all cases includes representatives of the provincial department of agriculture and the national employment service. In addition, in most provinces, representatives of farm organizations and other groups are also included in the membership of the committee. These committees are concerned not only with local and interprovincial recruitment and movement and' placement of farm workers, but also make recommendations relative to the importation of immigrant agricultural workers and their recommendations are cleared through the Department of Labour to the Department of Citizenship and Immigration which selects the immigrants overseas.

speechtext:
['No, not for the
government. Looking over the debates of the House of Commons of about 20 years ago, I came across precisely the same sort of debate we are having today, on the subject of unemployment, by way of an amendment to the motion to go into supply. I find that almost the same kind of thing was being said then as we have heard today.
For instance, at page 1275 of Hansard for April 4, 1930, I find a speech by my old friend Henry Spencer, in which he speaks of the unemployment situation and points out that at that time the number of unemployed in Canada stood, in round figures, at 100,000. That interested me, because at that time it was quite obvious that members of the house on all sides were taking the unemployment situation extremely seriously. Yet here we had a figure of 100,000 out of an admittedly lower population of about 10 million. That is, there was only a fifth of the number of
Proposed Committee on Unemployment unemployed we have today, at a time when the population was two-thirds of today's population.
Now, of course not all people at that time took the same serious view of the matter that Mr. Henry Spencer did. We had another gentleman who was, need I say, a government supporter of the day, a member of the Liberal party in 1930, and he had this to say in part, as reported at page 1347 of Hansard for April 7, 1930:
During the summer season of 1929 this country enjoyed the greatest era of prosperity that it had known since confederation. Never in the history of this nation have we enjoyed greater prosperity, greater development and greater contentment, and nowhere else in the world could a labouring class be found who enjoyed a higher standard of living than did the people of Canada during the year 1929.
Mr. Speaker, one might almost have imagined that the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Howe) was speaking. Yes; and then, as my Conservative friend says, "came the deluge". But the deluge was in the form of a Conservative government, which arrived in 1930. In Hansard for 1931 we have the report of speeches made at that time, in which the prime minister of the day is quoted as having said this, as reported at page 465:
I tell you that when parliament meets, if there is not then evident further increase in employment, additional steps will be taken to meet the situation.
And the hon. member who quoted him said this:
I believe, Mr. Speaker, we have a right to know what those additional steps are to be.
Again that is curiously reminiscent. I refer you, Mr. Speaker, to a more recent Hansard, as recent as February 12 of this year. At page 2026 we find a statement by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) in answer to a question regarding the fiscal and monetary measures which, according to the Acting Prime Minister, this government is now implementing to prevent a rise in the level of unemployment. I find in it very much the same sort of vague assurance that the people of Canada were receiving from their spokesmen in 1930 and 1931.
I suggest that it is time the government began to take a little serious interest in the actual state of affairs in Canada, that they should take their heads out of the sand, that they should, for instance, perhaps listen to the voice of the executive commission of the Canadian association of social workers whose corresponding secretary had a letter in the Toronto Globe and Mail this morning, from which I should like to quote a few rather striking sentences:
Last year, after most careful study by the Canadian Welfare Council and its membership across
2344	HOUSE OF
Proposed Committee on Unemployment
Canada, representations were made to the government at Ottawa and to all provincial governments regarding the urgent necessity of having some over-all and permanent provision made to meet the situation and avoid the destitution and disruption of normal family living which today faces many families through no fault of their own. As far as can be observed, nothing has been done to make effective the recommendations made in this report or to evolve any satisfactory alternatives. Unemployment of able-bodied employable people who need and want work is a national problem which strikes at the very roots of family life and causes untold suffering.
There is more in the same vein, Mr. Speaker, which indicates that people whose daily work brings them into close contact with the unemployed are viewing the situation today with a great deal more gravity than our spokesmen on the government benches are doing.
It may be that such champions of free enterprise as the government of Canada will pay more attention to such sturdy enterprises as Messrs. Dun and Bradstreet rather than to the presumably soft-hearted and sentimental social workers. Messrs. Dun and Bradstreet have some rather shattering information for us too, as published in the Financial Post of February 13 of this year, where they report the number of business failures in the years 1952 and 1953. They tell us that in 1952 we had 843 business failures; in 1953, 1,039, an increase of 23 per cent. But worse than that, the number of business failures in the last quarter of 1952 were 192. In the last quarter of 1953 there were 317 failures, an increase of 65 per cent.', "The liabilities of those failing concerns presented an even more serious picture. In 1952 the total liabilities of business failures amounted to $21,823,000. In 1953 the liabilities amounted to $30,704,000, an increase of 40 per cent. But here again we find that the final quarters of each year present an even more depressing picture. In the last quarter of 1952 the liabilities of business failures amounted to $4,605,000; whereas in the last quarter of 1953 the liabilities amounted to $10,325,000, an increase of 125 per cent.
Since it is ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I beg leave to move the adjournment of the debate.
On motion of Mr. Cameron (Nanaimo) the debate was adjourned."]

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, February 19, consideration of the motion of Mr. St. Laurent for the second reading of Bill No. 172, to amend the Salaries Act.

maintopic: OPPOSITION BY INDIA TO UNITED STATES SUPPLYING ARMS TO PAKISTAN
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE SALARIES OF MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether, in proposing this legislation, the members of the cabinet appreciate what their colleagues, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), are going to do to them as a result of this increase. It is apparent that the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Howe) has not yet realized the position because, speaking on Friday last, he said, as reported at page 2250 of Hansard:
Assuming that a minister is a married man with two dependent children, which may be flattering to some of my colleagues, his tax deduction today would be $3,700.
That may have been correct a week ago, but it was not correct on Friday when the Acting Prime Minister spoke.
According to my calculations, a married man with two dependent children, with no other income, would be liable to a tax of $5,375. I hope the Acting Prime Minister will check his figures. I am sure he has no one from the Department of National Revenue or his own bureau of statistics working out his income tax return, because there is a considerable difference between $5,375 and the figure the Acting Prime Minister

gave on Friday of $3,700. There is a difference, in fact, of $1,675, and the tax on the new amount will be $2,250. I am not suggesting that these are not sizeable amounts, but I have paid some attention to instructions regarding relevancy since Friday, Mr. Speaker, and if one gives consideration to the relevant amount the' present position is this.
A member of the cabinet who has no other income receives a salary on the present basis of $20,000, less $5,375 tax, which would leave $14,625, plus a car allowance of $2,000, which is not taxable, and he would have a total amount of $16,625, or $1,385 per month.
In all seriousness I want to suggest that when one is in a position of obtaining $1,385 per month one should ask oneself whether it is worth it to meet the criticism one must meet in order to receive an extra $230 per month.
I will concede that I do not know a member of the cabinet who would not be in a better position today than he is now if he had never entered public life; but a number of years ago, I am sure for very good reasons, the members of this cabinet decided to enter public life and I for one cannot express a great deal of sympathy for those who have missed making a great fortune.
In fact, I believe some of the unhappiest people I have ever known during my lifetime have been people who made the mistake of trying to accumulate money, and with few exceptions, whether they made a lot or very little money, they missed a great deal in life.
Even if the members of the cabinet were able to save every cent of this increase for ten years it would amount to only $27,500. Again I am not suggesting that is not a considerable sum, but it is a very small amount compared with the fantastic fortunes that have been made by some people in Canadian history.
There was the case of the member of the other place who died recently. In one report I saw his estate valued at $1,750,000 and in another it was estimated at $1,200,000. It takes a long time to save that amount of money even if one saved the entire indemnity of a senator, previous to the last increase. If a senator did not spend one cent of that $6,000, it would take 200 years saving that amount per year to accumulate $1,200,000.
I therefore suggest it is too late now for the members of the cabinet to feel sorry for themselves and to wonder what their position might have been if they had stayed
Salaries Act
out of public life and devoted their time to practising law or pursuing a business career or doing anything else that might enable them to accumulate a sizeable fortune.
It has been demonstrated in Canadian history that a cabinet can so organize the affairs of the country that we can plan our production and consumption with unemployment and a low standard of living, or full employment and a high standard of living. If the cabinet will so organize our affairs that we can have a high level of employment and a rising standard of living, then they will have no need to worry about the future.
If, on the other hand, our economy cannot be organized so we can have full employment and a high standard of living, then I submit that for them to try to put themselves in a preferred position is folly. I suggest it must be very difficult to explain how one cannot get along on $1,385 per month but that an additional $230 or a total of $1,615 per month after payment of tax would be adequate.
I wish to add before I conclude that I have a very high personal regard for the members of the cabinet. I have never thought that, because I am in opposition, my constituents have suffered. I feel sure that in spite of these critical remarks the views I express will not be held against my constituents when I have occasion to consult members of the cabinet in connection with various problems.

maintopic: OPPOSITION BY INDIA TO UNITED STATES SUPPLYING ARMS TO PAKISTAN
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE SALARIES OF MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to go on record, along with other hon. members, as opposing the bill now before the house for increasing by $5,000 a year the salaries of members of the cabinet. I also want to associate myself with those who have emphasized that their remarks were in no way directed against the persons who compose the present Canadian cabinet.
My opposition to this bill is based on my belief that this bill would not be in the best interests of the people of Canada if it were passed by parliament at this time. I believe hon. members should bear in mind, and I believe the cabinet should also remember this, that they are now assured of an increase in salary amounting to $4,000 a year because of the fact that they are members of parliament. Members of the cabinet will now receive a salary of $22,000 per year instead of $18,000 per year which prevailed when this parliament began.
I believe $22,000 a year is sufficient for a cabinet minister and in keeping with our concept of democracy and the present economic prospects for the rest of the people of this country. I can think of occasions when

Salaries Act
an increase in the salaries of cabinet ministers would be absolutely necessary. I believe such an increase would be necessary if we had gone through a period of violent inflation which had made the purchasing power of salaries so low that an increase became absolutely necessary. It is true that we have gone through a period of inflation. However, I believe the result of that inflation has been overcome, as far as the cabinet is concerned, to a considerable extent by the increase that has already been placed in effect. I would think, too, that it would be quite in order for the government to move an increase in cabinet ministers' salaries in keeping with general increases in the economic standard of living of the people of Canada. But it seems to me that at the present time the prospects for the average Canadian are perhaps for a lowering of the standard of living rather than for an increase in it.

maintopic: OPPOSITION BY INDIA TO UNITED STATES SUPPLYING ARMS TO PAKISTAN
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE SALARIES OF MINISTERS
speechtext: It has never been better.

maintopic: OPPOSITION BY INDIA TO UNITED STATES SUPPLYING ARMS TO PAKISTAN
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE SALARIES OF MINISTERS
speechtext:
Certainly the most optimistic prediction I have heard from any minister of the government is that the rate of improvement in our standard of living is likely to be less in the future than it has been in the recent past. I say that if the vast majority of Canadians could look forward to a continuing increase in the standard of living over the next few years, then perhaps a move like this one might be justified.
Just previous to the present debate we had a debate on unemployment. The business for the house today is, first, the measure we are now discussing, to be followed by a debate on unemployment. I cannot see any consistency in the proposal now advanced to increase the salaries of members of the government and I cannot understand how their arguments for an increase can be justified if they are to be followed in a few moments perhaps by the very opposite arguments against doing something immediate about unemployment. In other words, when unemployed workers come to the House of Commons and to parliament they are met by ministers of the government saying to them, "Your wages have gone up by a tremendous rate; you are helping to price yourselves out of the market; the best thing you can do is to change employment", and then the next time saying, "We need an increase in cabinet ministers' salaries".

maintopic: OPPOSITION BY INDIA TO UNITED STATES SUPPLYING ARMS TO PAKISTAN
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE SALARIES OF MINISTERS
speechtext: Is the hon. member suggesting a change of employment on the opposite side of the house?

maintopic: OPPOSITION BY INDIA TO UNITED STATES SUPPLYING ARMS TO PAKISTAN
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE SALARIES OF MINISTERS
speechtext:
That change might follow. I do not know. The public decided a year ago

that there should be no change in employment. Of course, I think the public came to their conclusion without the benefit of any advance knowledge of the bill now under discussion. Nevertheless, the country decided the political party that should form the government, and that political party will continue in office during this parliament. I do not know who is the author of the note that was just handed to me, but it says "They will price themselves out of the market". I do not know just what that means but at any rate it sounds like something I could support. To suggest an increase of $9,000 a year, made up of $4,000 increase as a member of parliament and $5,000 as a cabinet minister, is advancing a proposition that, at this stage in our economic development, is fantastic. People working in the farm implement industry have been told that their wages are too high in relation to the competitive position of the country. They have been told that $2.14 an hour for the members of that industry is a wage that has resulted in pricing themselves out of the market. A wage of $2.14 an hour in that industry means an income of $60 a week or $3,000 a year. This bill when enacted-if it is enacted-will result in a total increase of $9,000 a year; in other words, the amount of that increase is three times as much as the income of these individuals who were told, not so long ago, that their wages were at a point where they were pricing themselves out of the market.
I may not be the brightest student of economics but I cannot understand how one moment you can say to workers that $2.14 an hour is such a high wage that you are pricing yourselves out of the market and then come to parliament with a bill such as the one we have before us this afternoon.
The net income of farmers went down last year and the year before, 1952. The forecasts are that farm income in 1954 will go down. The forecasts are that the cost of living will level out or will go down. I for one believe that the present rate of pay, without this measure, to members of the government is sufficient. In a democracy such as ours I believe that members of the government-yes, members of parliament- should be paid an income in keeping with their responsibilities, if you like, one that will give them and their families, while they are carrying on in public life, an amount sufficient to remove severe financial worries. I imagine that it would be rather difficult to give your undivided attention to the needs of the country if you are compelled to consider your own economic situation and if you are faced with a good deal of worry

on that account. However, it seems to me that if this bill were turned down, the present state of affairs would give the cabinet ministers a reasonable remuneration.
I suppose that the personnel of the cabinet are like the personnel in the House of Commons, or in the C.C.F. group or that you may meet in any walk of life. You have the kind of people you have in a school class. You have good students, fair students and below average students. I suppose that in the cabinet there are cabinet ministers-I do not know which ones they are-who have not quite so much ability as have certain other cabinet ministers. But the cabinet ministers whom I see in the front row of the government benches this afternoon in this house could go out of parliament, I am sure, and earn far more than they will get even with the passage of this measure.

maintopic: OPPOSITION BY INDIA TO UNITED STATES SUPPLYING ARMS TO PAKISTAN
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE SALARIES OF MINISTERS
speechtext: Not all of them.

maintopic: OPPOSITION BY INDIA TO UNITED STATES SUPPLYING ARMS TO PAKISTAN
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE SALARIES OF MINISTERS
speechtext:
I said "those in the front row". I was being careful. I think I could perhaps even move into the second row and include the cabinet ministers that I .see in their seats there this afternoon. As I say, I do not know which ones you would put ahead of which other members of the cabinet, but I am sure that a great many of the cabinet ministers could in private life earn far more than they will get from the passage of this measure. So whether this bill is passed or not, it will not bring the same financial remuneration that they would have if they had not come into public service. I know that the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Howe)-and this is well known-could have continued to make far more in his private business than he could representing the country. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) came from a very responsible position, the premier of a province, into the cabinet. I believe that the members of the cabinet, yes members of parliament generally, come to parliament hoping that they will be able to render a public service by accepting such a position.
I do not really believe this increase will get better cabinet ministers. I do not believe it will result in getting cabinet ministers of any lesser ability than we now have. I do not believe people join a political party, run for office as members of parliament, and are accepted into the cabinet because of the pay that is involved. Rather, I think they accept those responsibilities in the hope that they will be rendering a service to their country. I feel that the remuneration now provided, without this measure, is in keeping with the responsibilities and the dignity of the position that they now have.

speechtext:
It has been said by several speakers that the glory of being a cabinet minister should be compensation enough; the salary should not matter. Perhaps it is enough for the head of the family; but is it enough for his wife and children? After all, most members of this cabinet are spending the most productive years of their lives in the service of the crown, years when I think all of them could be making provision not only for their old age but for the future and education of their family. I know from my experience in the cabinet over the years that the salaries are not sufficient in themselves to permit suitable provision for their wives and children.
People may think it is rather embarrassing for me to stand here and plead for a raise in pay for myself. I may say that this is not a movement by the cabinet as a whole. It is a movement by three or four older members of the cabinet who are not particularly concerned about their own salary, and who no longer have dependents. They are trying to right an injustice which has been allowed to continue far too long.
This is the fourth time since confederation that the salaries of cabinet ministers have been increased. They are not increased often. The period which has elapsed since the last increase is the longest by far of any of the periods during which cabinet ministers' salaries have been unchanged. The present salaries were fixed in 1920. When any changes have been made in the past, the increase has been about 50 per cent, and we are following that pattern once again. Does anyone know of any class of salaries that have not been increased by 50 per cent since 1920? I do not know of any class of salaries that have not. I believe that in fixing the rate of increase we have not only followed the pattern, but have made a reasonable adjustment of the salary scales referred to in the bill.
Mr. Bennett was discussing these very same salaries I am discussing today when he spoke back in 1931; and that was a year, as my hon. friends from Saskatchewan will know, when wheat was selling at 20 cents a bushel on the farms. This was what Mr. Bennett had to say, as it appears at page 4507 of Hansard for that year:
But it is unfair to ask men to leave their homes and their professions, in many instances their future, and come to the city of Ottawa and live

here, maintaining that position which they are bound to maintain by virtue of their office, and then find themselves, at the end of a term of office, hopelessly bankrupt. That has happened in this city. It has happened during the last few years that one of the leading ministers of the crown found himself in that position, and when he departed this life his estate indicated that that was so.
Men in politics should not be compelled to rely upon the benefaction of friends or otherwise, so far as the duty they owe the state is concerned; and when men serve Cans da for the miserable pittance they get, as compared with what they would receive if they were practising their professions-they would get twice as much-to say that they should come here and find themselves, after a term of office, with their little savings gone, with their families on the threshold of life, without much opportunity to get an education because of the cost, and then to expect them to maintain the dignity of their office, entertaining, dispensing hospitality, treating visitors as they should treat them, moving to and fro, from one place to another, maintaining ears, I do not believe that anybody would suggest that this is at all reasonable.
Mr. Bennett, speaking in 1931, was talking about present-day cabinet ministers' salaries. As I say, I think the comment that other systems should be reviewed is hardly one that would lead hon. members to vote against this measure.
I was very interested in what was said by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Mac-donnell), who said that he does not know enough about the salaries position to be able to vote for the bill, and that therefore he would vote against it. I would point out that the hon. member for many years was general manager of one of the greatest trust companies in the country, a company with branches from coast to coast; and I think if anyone should know about salaries, the hon. member for Greenwood should be that man-and about pensions, as well.
I hope the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) will not vote against the measure for the reason he is not sure we are not paying cabinet ministers too much. In his idle moments he can go out, after he has performed his duties as a member of parliament, and, as the head of one of the great pulp and paper companies in the country, draw a salary three or four times as great as the salaries we are discussing here.
I could pass along the same thought to several other members in the house. I see the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Nickle) in his seat. I hope he is not going to say that he will vote against the measure because he thinks no man can earn that much money. I could even find a member in the C.C.F. party who should not be appalled at the scale of salary indicated in the measure. I think he knows something about salaries as large as that, and that he has also earned as large a salary in his idle moments, after completing his duties here in the house.

However, I do not know that we want to pursue that point any farther. I was interested in the reason given by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) for not supporting the measure. He said he could not support it because he does not think the car allowance provision is legal. All we know about the car allowance legislation-and he tells us it was drafted by the present Auditor General-is that it was sponsored in the house by the then prime minister of Canada, who was certainly one of the great legal authorities of his generation. It has been passed upon from time to time by law officers of the crown. And, just to make sure, in the last two or three days I referred it to the law officers of the crown, and they tell me that the provision introduced by Mr. Bennett, in 1931, is a continuing provision that will be the law of the land until it is repealed by parliament. The argument that it could be regarded as a temporary measure is one that would convince no one, except the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
It has been suggested by others that if we pass the bill it will upset the welfare legislation that we have enacted. I have heard some statements about unemployment insurance payments. I have heard it suggested that the $24 a week unemployment insurance payment, what has been described as a mere pittance, will be cut if this bill is passed. I have heard it suggested that payments to veterans will be cut, and that somehow this bill is going to affect payments to the blind. I did not hear a similar reference with regard to family allowances; I am sure hon. members must have overlooked them. Let me give an assurance that none of those benefits will be cut if this bill passes the house.
It has been suggested by the leader of the C.C.F. party that he speaks for his group in opposing the measure.

Mr. Chairman, when the Acting Prime Minister spoke a few moments ago he made two statements to which I must take exception. I think he will be the first to admit that when I began my remarks on Friday I indicated my opposition to the bill was in relation to its substance. I am opposed to the proposed increases. The other statement which the Acting Prime Minister made to which I must take exception was his remark that I had alleged that the paying of the motorcar allowance was illegal. Had it not been for the fact that I knew we would shortly be in committee of the whole when I would be able to deal with the point I would have raised a point of order or a question of privilege at that time. I felt that this was the easier way to do it. I would remind the Acting Prime Minister that when I discussed this question of the motorcar allowance on Friday, February 19, I said, as reported on page 2259 of Hansard:

If it were the Auditor General would have said so long ago. But I am asserting in the words of the Auditor General that although it may be proper

to deal with a transitory matter by means of items in the estimates, it is not fair to parliament nor to the recipients to continue year after year making payments of this kind on the basis of an item in the Appropriation Act of 1931, which was spent long ago.
I certainly do not intend to take the time of the committee in repeating the arguments which I advanced on Friday of last week, but I would remind the government that Mr. Watson Sellar, the Auditor General, made it perfectly clear that although this practice was legal it had undesirable characteristics, that it was not the proper way to make a payment which is to be made year after year and that it should be dealt with in some other manner. The Auditor General has suggested two or three times that there were other ways in which an item such as this should be handled.
Just in case you may be wondering, Mr. Chairman, and it would be a perfectly proper point for you to wonder about, how this question of motorcar allowances comes in in relation to the salaries of ministers, I would point out to you and to members of the committee generally that the bill before us is to amend the Salaries Act. That act now provides for each minister a salary of $10,000, but if you open the blue book of estimates to the first item of any department-

The answer the Prime Minister gave, as reported at page 4970 of Hansard, is as follows:
Progress is being made, but we have not yet reached the end we shall have achieved when the progress has been completed.
Well, of course, that produced a laugh in the house and brought that particular exchange to an end, but I dared to hope that it signified that attention was being given to the point. I see that attention has been given to one of these matters and we are being asked to deal with it in this bill. That comes up under the next clause. But this one has not been touched. I had hoped that consideration might be given to this matter over the week end and that that consideration would result in a willingness on the part of the government to deal with it in this statute. The words of the Acting Prime Minister a few

moments ago do not suggest that that has been the result of such thinking, though I still hope it might be considered.
If the government is not prepared to make this change by a change in the Salaries Act, then I ask that consideration be given to separating the motorcar allowance from the salaries in the estimates, and putting it in as an item that we can vote every year, in the same way in which we vote an item covering the extra $4,000 paid to parliamentary assistants. If the situation is not to be dealt with in a more satisfactory manner than has been the case thus far, I would like to hear from the Acting Prime Minister, or the Minister of Finance, or any other member of the cabinet who wishes to answer the question, as to when and by whom the decision was made that this motorcar allowance was to be free of income tax.

Mr. Chairman, the point at issue is an interesting one. It is really a battle between legal giants. As 1 said, the statute was framed by Mr. R. B. Bennett, when he was prime minister, and it has been discussed by Mr. St. Laurent, who is also a legal authority. My hon. friend, on the basis of his legal training and experience, does not like it. I do not know that we can do much about it. We are told that this statute is a statute of Canada and it is binding until it is repealed. The purpose of this bill is not to repeal it. This is a separate piece of legislation. The hon. member asks why the allowance is tax-free. The answer is, because it was voted to cover an expenditure for a definite purpose. Before 1931, from the time when automobiles were invented, each minister of the crown had an automobile and a chauffeur at his disposal. That is still true in most of the countries I have visited. I do not think I have ever been in a country where members of the government were not furnished with motorcars and drivers. We do not have that provision here and I personally am not sorry. If we have an official visitor I can lend him my car, providing my wife is not using it and I do not require it. Otherwise he would have to travel by taxi. That is all right, but in 1931 it was not the desire to lower, if you like, the standard of government representation, and it was the intention to do away with that practice of providing automobiles and instead make an allowance which could be used for the purpose indicated.
(Mr. Knowles.]
An expenditure of that kind is, of course, when properly authorized, not taxable and that is the reason an expenditure for a definite purpose by a minister is tax free. My hon. friend will realize that even parliamentary salaries paid to members of parliament include $2,000 which is set aside as an expense account and it is not taxed. The two items are on a par. An hon. member not a member of the government receives $2,000 which is set aside for his expenses and a minister receives $2,000 which is set aside for automobile expense.

In this particular case there are at least two of us in this group who are trying to do our own thinking. However, putting this increase for cabinet ministers on the basis of income or salary is in my opinion basing it on the wrong premise. I believe the Acting Prime Minister put it in its proper perspective when he said the cabinet minister's indemnity is a compensation which permits him to meet the commitments imposed upon him because of the office he occupies.
Commitments made by cabinet ministers or by members of this house are not organized or brought about by themselves. They are commitments that are organized for them by someone else. They are passed on to you. You meet the bill whether you like it or not. I have never looked upon the compensation paid either to members or to the cabinet as being a matter of salaries. It is a straight matter of enabling you to meet your commitments.
As the Acting Prime Minister pointed out, there is only one thing wrong with this legislation, namely that it should have been brought in in 1941 or 1942. That is when it should have been brought in. I think the cabinet of that day and the prime minister of that day missed the boat. I am sure that most hon. members who take a reasonable view of the matter will agree that, after a lapse of 33 years, it is time there was an adjustment in the indemnities that are paid in this house, all round. As far as the cabinet is concerned, that indemnity was fixed back in 1933, when their commitments were relatively simple compared with what you have got to meet today. As far as I am concerned, I am going to say this quite
Salaries Act
frankly. I would not accept a cabinet post for any money, because no money could compensate you for the misery you are obliged to go through; and I have seen enough of it. You go to a dinner; it is a delegation; and you pay for the dinner, generally. You go to a luncheon; it is a delegation; and the same thing occurs. Then someone out in Vancouver decides that they want you in Vancouver, so you go to Vancouver whether you like it or not and you pay the shot for what it costs you. If you are wanted down in Nova Scotia, you do the same thing whether you like it or not or whether it is important or not. You get the call and you go.
When you get right down to it, on the question ''Will you run?" there are members of this cabinet who were drafted since I came into this house. The Prime Minister was drafted. There is not any question about that fact. I was here when he first came into the house and took over the justice portfolio. At that time he made it quite clear that the end of the war was the end of his term, and that he came in for the purpose of making his contribution towards the war. We all know-those who are honest enough to admit it-that he wanted to get out when the war was over but that he was "pressured" into staying by a large number of people in this country.
The Minister of Labour was drafted. He was taken in in the same way. He was given a cabinet post before he came into the house. If members are thinking in terms of the future of this country and not in terms of votes, they will take the view that any reasonable person will take when he considers this fact. Back in 1931 when the indemnity was fixed, you came in here, took a cabinet post and ran the little show that was going on in Canada, with a billion dollars or so of gross national product. It was a relatively simple matter to administer the affairs of Canada at that time. But it is not so simple today, as will be seen when you take a look at the expenditures for veterans, pensions and social security measures you have gone into. Those are perhaps not so hard to handle but when you take a look at the development of T.C.A., you will realize that you must have in the cabinet someone who knows something about Trans-Canada Air Lines. You cannot just pick up somebody off the street and send him in to supervise that vast organization under which comes steamships, Canadian National Railways and Trans-Canada Air Lines. There must be someone in there who knows something about these matters.
Again, consider the development of Polymer Corporation. You have to have someone

Salaries Act
in the cabinet who knows something about it. When the present Acting Prime Minister decides to hang up the boxing gloves, I sometimes wonder how long we are going to hold on to some of these crown companies that were developed with a great deal of opposition from the outside, and also from the inside in this chamber. You are going to need someone in there who knows something about that Polymer set-up and the value it will have to Canada in the future. We do not want to find ourselves in our bare feet, for want of rubber, again in the middle of a war -as happened last time-while the synthetic formula that was held in the United States was sent over and given to the Germans when Burma fell and the rest of our rubber resources were folding up. The Acting Prime Minister I think was the prime mover in the development of Polymer. It is a big job to watch that organization and to see that it makes proper progress.
The situation is the same with regard to Canadian Arsenals, the basis of the munitions industry, something that we in this group all fought for. Today it is doing most of the research in developing patents for small arms, munitions, and so forth. You want in the cabinet somebody who is going to be able to make a fair appraisal of that kind of organization.
I do not look upon the amount of money involved today as a salary or as a compensation for the job at all. I think you are recognizing the fact that since the indemnity was set, the commitments that a cabinet minister has to meet have gone up not by 50 per cent but by 500 per cent; and that is not saying anything at all about the work involved. You are now making an attempt to adjust the matter. I want to say this also. If we want to be fair, we will realize that there are not many members in that cabinet who are going to enjoy that income for very long. They are all about in the same position as that in which I am, thinking about hanging up the boxing gloves and playing with their grandchildren.

I believe that the cabinet today is doing something that is going to be of benefit to those who may come after us. What did we have to do during the war when we swung over into a planned economy? You did not pick technicians out of the air. Someone had to run the show, and it had to be someone who knew something about it. We had to go to industry all across this country. When the government went into a partially planned economy, at least to plan the war, they had to go out

and take technicians from all over the country, from industry and from commerce, establishing everything that was needed by way of technical services, and they had to pay them. It is not reasonable for us to take the position that, when we take a man like Donald Gordon, say to him, "You run the Canadian National Railways" and pay him $50,000 a year, yet as to the man who supervises the operation, namely the Minister of Transport, $10,000 is good enough for him. Why the difference? Who is working for whom? Who is supposed to be the best qualified person? I think the man who supervises the whole set-up and is responsible to the people of Canada has the greatest responsibility. He has to have a great deal of knowledge.
Then there is the governor of the Bank of Canada, and his assistant. You pay him $30,000 a year. The Minister of Finance is his boss. So the boss works for $10,000 and the man he is bossing is entitled to $30,000. And so it goes right on through your civil service in the top brackets. I rise particularly, Mr. Chairman, to deal with a remark made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South concerning a motion that is before the house in regard to another subject matter. He stated that if I had been here the motion would not have been introduced, referring to the question of unemployment. Might I assure the hon. member that if I had been here I would have introduced the motion myself. There was no agreement, there was no understanding, and it would have been entirely inconsistent with what has taken place in this house if the opposition, which has been constantly demanding action to create employment, had not been the party to raise the motion that was raised. I most certainly would have presented it myself had I been here.
May I say to the bubbling Secretary of State, who finds this so amusing, that he may well recall some of the statements already on the record concerning what the predecessor of the present Prime Minister had to say about this same problem on an earlier occasion. He might bear in mind his close association with those facts, perhaps even some of the words, when he deals with the subject so lightly on this occasion.
Salaries Act
I want to refer briefly to the point that has been made. I must say that what has been said by the hon. member who just sat down must be music to the ears of the Acting Prime Minister, and it certainly was obviously music to the ears of hon. members opposite. It is indeed special pleading of a very interesting kind in support of the measure that is now before us. In so far as this party is concerned, the arguments that have been presented have not been inconsistent with anything that may be said about the dignity of the office of prime minister or any member of the government.
We have made it quite clear that we recognize the need for the service in government of men of the highest ability. The position we have taken is that this is something that calls for examination and inquiry as to the best way in which it should be done. We are not bound by the precedents of Westminster by any manner of means. Nevertheless, we have borrowed our whole parliamentary system from Westminster, and have not hesitated to admit that fact. On many occasions the present Prime Minister has made it clear that he recognizes our debt to Westminster in that respect.
It may be notable that only within the last few days a select committee appointed by that house has been dealing with the very problem we have been discussing here. This committee has made recommendations, and those recommendations have already raised a storm in Britain, not merely because the amounts are to be increased but because of the belief that it is inappropriate to deal with the subject in this way without due regard to the wider factors that are before them.
There are alternative methods of recognizing executive ability. I have no doubt that the hon. member who just sat down would be the last to suggest that every union organizer in this country receives the same remuneration. Experience and responsibility do count, and the very nature of the office has some bearing on the amount that will be received. I believe we are in agreement on the basic considerations. Having accepted that proposition, and taking the argument of the Prime Minister that we should examine this from the point of view of recognizing executive ability, then I can only go one step farther and say that executive ability is not recognized by the same flat salary. It is recognized by seeking to make the salary an amount that will be in keeping with the responsibilities.

I would simply point out that what we have sought to do is make it clear to the house that when hon. members are telling other people, who are dependent upon decisions of parliament, that we must be fully informed in regard to all the facts before we act in any of those matters, that is the very time we ourselves should be fully informed in regard to any possible alternative, or as to the right figures that should be dealt with.

We have suggested one way in which this can be done. We have made it clear that we will support the idea of either a royal commission or a select committee of the house. Either method would be following the same procedure which has been so satisfactory in relation to other proceedings in this house and in relation to proceedings of this very kind at Westminster, from which we have borrowed so many of our practices.
I can only repeat what I have said before, that if we followed this course we would in no way be shelving responsibility. No royal commission or select committee can make any legislative decisions. I have simply proposed in relation to this measure, and in relation to another measure with which we dealt on an earlier occasion, that we should, when this whole matter is under review, follow the wise and sensible course of examining the possibility of arriving at figures by some consideration of what the real factors actually are. Then in reaching this decision we would be able to say that we followed the same tests in reaching conclusions as we apply over and over again when other people depending upon the decisions of parliament ask us for consideration.

But when things are done as they are now I have no hesitation whatsoever in criticizing.
Just let me state one point here. It may not be particularly germane to the bill, but the fact is that up to now not much of what has been said has been germane. What is the record of this government? One of the last acts of the Conservative regime, when it went out of office in 1935, was to put an Unemployment Insurance Act on the statute books of Canada. The Liberal party of that day opposed the passage of that act because they said it was ultra vires of the dominion government. When the Liberals came into office they referred it to the courts, and that is how it was found to be.
But did the Liberal government bring in an unemployment insurance act in 1937? No. Did they bring in an unemployment insurance act in 1938? No. Did they bring in an unemployment insurance act in 1939? No. Did they seek an amendment to the constitution in order to bring one in? No. But they sought an amendment in 1940, and later introduced an unemployment insurance bill. When it was introduced it was not as a social security measure; it came in as an anti-inflationary measure.
And so here is the government's record in regard to unemployment and conditions in the country from 1935 to 1940. They could not put unemployment insurance into effect until recruiting for the armed services and war industries had taken sufficient workers off the unemployment rolls. There you have the picture.

speechtext:
I agree with you, Mr. Chairman. I am out of order; and the speakers who preceded me were out of order. The main point I want to make is that when we are debating these matters we should take it for granted that one is motivated by good intentions. If anybody feels that his conscience pricks him, and because of that he must justify himself, that is all right; he must salve his conscience in some way, but I am not in that position.
One thing I do know is the feeling of the people of the country. I know the feeling of the people in my own constituency, and I know that the feeling of the people in Vancouver is no different from that of the people in Halifax, in Toronto or anywhere else. Seventy-five per cent of them are in opposition to these increases which we are putting into effect. Surely what we are doing here is relevant to unemployment, to old age pensions and to other things. If I were sent here at all I was sent for the one purpose of raising the standard of living of those whose standard of living is low. I was not sent here-and I am not going to stay here under false pretences by giving the impression that I was- to raise our own indemnities and the salaries of the cabinet ministers. I have nothing to gain from opposing these increases. Nothing has been offered to me and I would not accept it anyway. Therefore I have not that to worry about.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: OPPOSITION BY INDIA TO UNITED STATES SUPPLYING ARMS TO PAKISTAN
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE SALARIES OF MINISTERS
speechtext:
I had not really intended to say anything in this debate, because among other things it is always a little more difficult to talk about matters that concern yourself. I am sorry the discussion has taken just the turn it has. Hypocrisy is not a human quality that I particularly admire, and I try not to practise it myself. Therefore let me say without hesitation that so far as I am concerned I feel that I have been underpaid ever since I have been here.
I readily concede that a man in public life should not be able to command as high a financial return as he might if he stayed outside. I think if we had to rely on the services of men who would only come to parliament or serve in the government if they could get a financial return as high as they could get outside, we would be deprived of the service in public life of some people that we ought to have. I readily concede that to those of us who are in public life there are great compensations other than the financial returns that we get. There is the satisfaction of public service performed and then to put it on the lower ground, the contacts that we make,
[The Deputy Chairman.]
the speeches that we deliver here in the House of Commons and the hands that we shake around the country. All that, I know, gives a great personal satisfaction to some of us. It keeps us in the public eye and we probably like that, some perhaps more than others.
But, as the Acting Prime Minister said, all of us, or most of us at any rate, have responsibilities to some people other than ourselves. I think some of those people do not derive the personal satisfactions out of public life that those of us who are in the forefront of it get, and I personally feel that there should not be too great a difference between what a man can command in the public service and what he can get outside.
That is important in order that we should be able to attract men to public life at a reasonably early age. They should not have to wait until they have made the future of their families and dependents secure before they enter public life. And even more important, they should not have to be dependent upon assistance from those who are outside parliament. I can only speak from personal experience, and I always hesitate to do this, but I live fairly modestly, as those of you who know me are aware. I have gone behind just a little bit every year since I have been here, and I have had to use such other modest resources as I might have. I do not think that is a good thing for public life, and I for one will never use the argument that because a man who is in a particular occupation averages only $3,000 or $4,000 a year a cabinet minister should not get more.
We all know that there are inequalities in life. Perhaps it is unfair that there should be, but we all know that even the leaders of great labour unions make a great deal more than cabinet ministers, and I daresay earn it. We all know, as the Acting Prime Minister has said, that men in relatively junior positions in industry, in commerce, make more than cabinet ministers will make even after the proposed increase. Therefore I make no point about that, Mr. Chairman. I say quite frankly that I think the proposed increase is fully justified.
I can understand the position taken by people who say that the increase is too much, and I am not questioning their bona fides in saying that. I find a little more difficulty in understanding the position taken by the official opposition. Most of the members of the official opposition-perhaps not all-are sufficiently experienced in public life, in business or in the professions to know first what responsibilities are incurred by a man in public life; and second, what the remuneration is for men of comparable ability in

the outside professions or occupations. Therefore I fail to see how anyone as experienced as my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition, my friends the hon. member for Greenwood, the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe, to mention only a few that I see sitting in front of me, could get any information from a royal commission as to what the appropriate salary should be for a man carrying on the executive responsibilities of a member of the government.
I also cannot agree with the Leader of the Opposition that there should be a difference in salaries between ministers. It may be true, and no doubt is true, that certain departments carry heavier administrative responsibilities than others, but every member of the government has to share in the collective responsibility for government policy, and so far as I know there has never been in Canada in any of the provincial governments, and certainly not in the federal government, any difference between the salaries of various members of the privy council.

I have not those figures
readily available, but of course in a good many of the crown corporations there are salaries substantially in excess of $10,000. I think I should indicate that there is perhaps some relevance between salaries paid to cabinet ministers and those paid to a number of top-level civil servants, and it tends to establish a ceiling which may not be desirable. I am talking of those in the higher ranks of the civil service. So I think it is fair to say that the salaries paid to ministers has some relevance at any rate to those paid to the permanent heads of departments.
Salaries Act

speechtext:
The reason I want the information is that I think the people of Canada should know the relevancy between the salaries of the cabinet and of other civil servants or executives in crown corporations. As I said before, if there is any failure within the civil service in any department of government or in a crown corporation, those men can resign and get out and the government will have to take the punishment. In the final analysis, the responsibility for success or failure in connection with all these things is upon the government and the responsible ministers.
I did not ask the question merely because I wanted that information only; and I am in full agreement with what the minister has said, but some of the average Joes in the country have said that it looks as though this is quite a jump the cabinet are making in their salaries. If those salaries can be compared with other salaries within their range or higher, then the people should know. I should like it to be on the record so the people of Canada may know. Perhaps I could put a question on the order paper, although it might not meet with the approval of the government to answer. Perhaps I shall put it on anyway and see what happens. Could the minister tell us how these salaries compare with the salaries of deputy ministers? Is the salary of any deputy minister higher than the salary of his minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: OPPOSITION BY INDIA TO UNITED STATES SUPPLYING ARMS TO PAKISTAN
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE SALARIES OF MINISTERS
speechtext:
Yes. The salaries of deputy ministers are public knowledge. Of course the salaries of officers of crown corporations are not public knowledge. I was going to wait until my hon. friend was finished, but if he will allow me perhaps I could give the reason they are not published.
Certain salaries, such as those of the deputy governor and the governor of the Bank of Canada have been made available, and that of the chairman of the Canadian National Railways; but the salaries of ordinary executive officers in crown corporations like Polymer, Canadian National Railways and so on are not made public. The reason is that the salaries of similar officers or executives, say in the Canadian Pacific Railway Company or one of the chartered banks or any commercial company, are not made public. These men say, "Well, if I work for the one company the salary I am

Salaries Act
paid is my own business, but it I work for this company it is to be made public". There is a certain amount of natural human reluctance to having salaries made public.
I am not arguing the point now, but it does affect the ability of the government to get good executives if they are not required to subject themselves to the rule in the public service that salaries be made public. In other words, we are competing with private industry for executives of this type.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE SALARIES OF MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall be very brief but nonetheless very emphatic in stating my opposition to this bill. I do not want to be over-harsh in my statements, but I think it must be generally agreed throughout the country that this matter has met with tremendous disfavour on the part of the people. What I have to say is in no way a reflection on the cabinet ministers now sitting on the other side of the house. As far as I am personally concerned I believe that they are responsible members, that they are competent, that they carry out their work to the best of their abilities, with a tremendous fidelity to their duty.
However, when I consider this matter I can only come to the conclusion that it is most inopportune at this time. I am quite certain that had the people of this country known prior to August 10 that the government contemplated any such move there would be many members in this house who are not present here today.
The hon. member for Macleod has endeavoured to find out what income is received by certain other people in order to arrive at a decision. I have here a table of incomes received by the Canadian people according to the income tax returns for 1951. A salary of $25,000 would be comparable with those provided under this bill, and according to this table only 8,260 people in Canada received an income of over $25,000 in 1951. In other words, only two-tenths of one per cent of the people of Canada in 1951 had incomes which were comparable to those provided for in the schedule to this bill.
When one considers the former measure which was passed he must realize that a cabinet minister is receiving a considerable amount of additional income which by fair deduction should constitute a fair return. The

salary of a cabinet minister has been increased to $12,000 by an additional $4,000 as a member of parliament. Under the new schedule a cabinet minister will have a salary of $15,000, a total indemnity of $8,000, a motorcar allowance of $2,000 and $2,000 tax-free expenses, or a total of $27,000. In my opinion that is fantastic when we consider the incomes reported by people throughout the country.
I do not agree with the hon. member for Cape Breton South, who has come to his own conclusion based on his own calculations. I think that as far as parliament is concerned, when we hope that democracy will be accepted as the finest form of government it will be detrimental if we as parliamentarians agree to an increase of this kind in the salaries of cabinet ministers.
When we come asking for increases in old age pensions, veterans allowances, mothers' allowances and so forth, the question is always asked in the house, "What about the cost of living?". We even had increases in civil servants salaries to keep pace with the increase in the cost of living. But in this bill the government comes to this house and asks for an increase not on the basis of any cost of living, but of a straight $9,000 for cabinet ministers.
I believe it is fantastic, Mr. Chairman, that we should be asked to support a measure of this kind. I do not believe it is in the interests of the government or in the interests of our people. I had a letter today informing me that 500 people have been thrown out of work at the Kitimat project. When it is recognized that there are over 500,000 unemployed in this country I say this is a most inopportune moment to introduce a bill of this nature, and I intend to vote against it.

maintopic: OPPOSITION BY INDIA TO UNITED STATES SUPPLYING ARMS TO PAKISTAN
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE SALARIES OF MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am quite sure everyone appreciates the Minister of Finance's approach to this problem and the straightforward and frank way in which he has dealt with it. I will not say that we all agree with him, but I am quite sure we do appreciate the basis on which he has considered it.
There was one thing he said however, which I think deserves some reply. He stated, for instance, that no one here would suggest that the salaries of cabinet ministers might be investigated by a royal commission or even a select committee of this house. Let me give the minister an example based on the proposed new clause 5 which is part of the bill we are now considering. That clause if carried will provide a salary of $15,000 per annum for the Solicitor General of Canada.

It may be, and I would ask the Minister of Finance if he does not think there is some merit in this suggestion, that there are members who would take particular exception to that provision. I believe there is some merit in examining this question, and I will advance the reasons why I think that provision should be brought into question.
What will happen in this case is that we will be battling out this question on the floor of the house. I have chosen this particular example to some extent deliberately, because the person holding that office is not in this house at all. Hon. members will have to battle across the floor of the house on the question of what should be the salary of a particular individual who is not in the house. I do not care on how high a plane you try to put it because it comes down to this, that if any one of us here were to say that this ex-cabinet minister or simply "X" should not have $15,000 a year but only $12,500, then you might talk until you are blue in the face without resolving the matter.
Of course I have nothing personal against the hon. gentleman who holds that position, but I am thinking of the position of a man who is not in the House of Commons and how extremely difficult it is to deal with the matter fairly, just as it is extremely difficult to be impartial about the matter of our own indemnities when it has to be battled out across the floor of the house.
Surely there could be no clearer reason why this matter should be considered by some such body as a royal commission or a parliamentary committee. I understand that in the United Kingdom they had before a committee, on a sort of oft the record basis, as it were, a number of individual members and ministers who gave them the facts concerning their own cases, so that the committee accumulated, based on their approach to the problem, the actual facts drawn from the personal experience of the ministers or members.
The Minister of Finance has himself told us how much he dislikes speaking of his personal experience in a matter of this kind. Of course he does, and I do not blame him. It must be most distasteful; yet he had to do it in order to justify the increase. I cannot think of a clearer reason than that advanced by the Minister of Finance himself as to why this question should be tackled, initially at any rate, upon the basis we have suggested. It is not on the basis that we might relieve ourselves of something that must become distasteful that we make this suggestion, but in order to arrive at a sounder basis for a decision.
Salaries Act
Reverting now to the question of the salary of the Solicitor General, I believe there might well be reasons why this office should not receive the salary which is now to be attached to it. The Solicitor General is not even a member of the cabinet. He is not a cabinet minister.

The governor in council may appoint an officer who shall be called the Solicitor General of Canada and who shall assist the Minister of Justice in the counsel work of the Department of Justice, and shall be charged with such other duties as are at any time assigned to him by the governor in council.
Now, it may be true that the person who holds the post of Solicitor General is, in another capacity, a privy councillor or a member of the cabinet. I am not denying that; but the post of Solicitor General is not a cabinet post.

The Solicitor General has been so called by His Excellency the Governor General, and he is just as much a member of the cabinet as I am.

speechtext: That is the point I am trying to make. The person who has the post may be a member of the cabinet, but the post of Solicitor General is not one which by any stretch of the imagination could be said to be within the definition of a cabinet post.

speechtext:
I believe the courts would take judicial notice of what is a cabinet minister, and the head of a department in ordinary parlance, in my understanding, is understood to be a cabinet minister. Despite the different view expressed by the Acting Prime Minister I suggest that in ordinary parlance the post of Solicitor General is not what would commonly be called a cabinet post. Certainly the duties of the Solicitor General as defined here raise some question, I believe, as to whether that post alone should carry

Salaries Act
with it the same salary as that which is attached to other cabinet posts, such as the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of National Defence.
It may well be that the time has arrived in the expansion and growth of Canada, and considering the role we have now assumed in international affairs, coupled with the new problems which are arising, when the number comprising the government should be increased, and that they should not all necessarily be of a cabinet rank carrying the same salary as senior ministers. It may be there should be some measure of reorganization along these lines. It certainly cannot be denied that at the present time some departments carry responsibilities in the national picture which make them more important than others.
These things, and the salaries to be attached to such posts as may be designated or recommended, are it seems to me subjects for inquiry by a royal commission or a select committee of this house. We might then determine whether a position involving a lesser degree of responsibility should carry the same salary, simply because at the present time it happens to carry with it a cabinet position, as that accorded to a ministerial post with a great deal heavier responsibility.

I was opposed to clause 1, as hon. members know, but I support clause 2 because it is an instance where an untidy way of dealing with a matter has been cleared up. For many years the Salaries Act has said that the secretary of the governor general was to be paid $2,400 a year. Apparently it was thought that was not enough and provision has been made for him to receive a salary of $10,000 a year. But instead of changing the statute it was done by putting an amount of $7,600 in the estimates each year. In other words, this person received two salaries, despite what the Minister of Finance said a moment ago.
I think it should be kept clear that there is no general rule that says people cannot receive two government salaries or two government cheques. There has to be a special rule in every case. Without commenting on the amount of this salary, I am glad that this matter has been tidied up and that from here on the salary of the secretary to the Governor General will be provided in one place. I may say, however, that I am disappointed that that same tidying up process was not carried through with reference to the question of motorcar allowances.
I have one other question with respect to this item. Perhaps I might address it to the Minister of Finance. We have had before us, a few days ago and today, two bills, namely Bills Nos. 171 and 172, that make certain changes in the indemnities of members and senators, in the salaries of ministers and so on. In connection with this question of the salary of the secretary to the Governor General, I notice that the estimates for 1954-55 anticipate the passing of Bill No. 172. Personally I think that procedure is inappropriate. I do not believe the people who drew up the book of estimates should have taken it for granted that any bill brought in by the government would go through. In practice I suppose that does happen, but how does it come about that in one instance it was anticipated that the bill would go through, but not in the other instances?
