there is a question I should like to ask, and it can be directed either to the Minister of Finance or to the Acting Prime Minister. I think I have made my position against this bill, with its increases, sufficiently clear that I will not be misunderstood if I draw attention to the fact that there seems to be one place where the increase has been overlooked. As the members of the government will notice, the bill now before us-I refer to the bill to amend the Salaries Act-makes no reference to the Minister of Defence Production. There is a reference to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and of course that is the item under which the minister in question draws his salary. As for the Minister of Defence Production, that salary is set out in the Defence Production Act. I think I should read the appropriate lines- they are very brief-of section 3 of the Defence Production Act. There is the usual wording "There shall be a department" and then subsection 2 of section 3 says this:
The salary of the minister, unless he is in receipt of a salary as the minister of another department of the government of Canada, shall be $10,000 per annum.
For all practical purposes, at least so far as the present situation is concerned, there is no need to amend subsection 2 of section 3 of the Defence Production Act because the Minister of Defence Production is not drawing that salary. He is drawing his salary as Minister of Trade and Commerce. But just suppose that the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Defence Production divided himself in two or suppose that the portfolios were divided, and that one portfolio were given to someone else. Unless the law were changed we would find that the Minister of Defence Production would be paid only $10,000 as opposed to $15,000 for the other ministers.
The answer to this anomaly may be that it is the intention to wind up the Department of Defence Production, or maybe it is another
Salaries Act
of those oversights. I am not arguing that this amount should be increased. I think the others should have been kept down to the $10,000 figure. However, I should be interested in an explanation of this point.

speechtext:
Before the adjournment of this debate on Wednesday of last week, I expressed my pleasure that at long last the members of the cabinet had agreed that in Canada we had over half a million unemployed. I find that admission on page 2085 of Hansard for February 15, 1954, when the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) said that the number of applications for jobs listed with the national employment services offices across Canada was 524,000 on January 21, 1954. However,
I regret that following that statement, as recorded on page 2088 of Hansard he said he did not believe there were that many unemployed in Canada. He said he felt our national unemployment estimate for this year was greater than those who were actually out of work.


I regret that very much, because for a number of weeks now the leaders of labour unions in the dominion had been saying that Canada had over half a million unemployed. We were informed for some time in this house that those union leaders did not know what they were talking about; that they were exaggerating the situation, and that unemployment had not nearly reached that stage. I notice that it is agreed by most responsible people in Canada that the union leaders were quite accurate in the statements they made.
I think the qualification the Minister of Labour made ignores a number of other factors. I know quite well that not everyone applying for a job would be in a position to accept it if he were offered a job a few days later. However, there are also thousands of people in Canada who do not register for employment with the unemployment insurance commission, yet they are looking for work. Think of all the people who have reached 35 or 40; we know that thousands of them have long since given up any hope of finding help at the offices of the local unemployment commission. They are not on record. What about those people whose unemployment insurance benefits have expired? Some of them have long since been taken off the record.
X believe a good idea of the extent of unemployment in Canada can be gained when we look at the census report for 1951. We find the labour force listed at just slightly over 4 million. Of those 4 million people, half a million in the course of that year earned less than $500. Another half million people earned between $500 and $1,000. In other words, almost 1 million people out of the 4 million total working force in that year earned less than $1,000. I believe that indicates there must have been a great deal more unemployment in 1951 than any of the statistics we had revealed. We can take the taxation statistics and see that in the taxation year 1951 about 42-8 per cent of the people of Canada earned less than $2,000 per year. When the average wage earner earns less than $2,000 per year, and when we know the average weekly wage in industry, it indicates that the average wage earner has been unemployed for almost half of that year.
I said that I was happy that at last the integrity of our labour leaders in Canada had been established. I prefer to accept the statement of our democratically elected labour leaders in Canada to the statements we sometimes hear from other would-be responsible people. For example, I cannot agree at all with the statements made by one spokesman

of the Liberal party who occupies a seat right next to that of a cabinet minister. On page 2132 of Hansard for February 16, 1954, he made an attack on the labour unions in this country. I have noticed that three Liberal spokesmen have followed the hon. member, and not one has denied that this hon. member spoke on behalf of the Liberal party. In referring to the labour leaders this hon. member said that they blamed everybody for their own mistakes.
In this section of the house we are not particularly blaming anyone for the incidence of unemployment. In this unplanned economy of ours, unemployment is inevitable. That has always been our contention and will continue to be our contention.

speechtext:
Upon returning from a week end in Toronto I found a telegram on my desk which had something to do with the unemployment situation. Just a few moments ago I indicated how the statements of our responsible labour leaders had been vindicated by statistics. Turning to the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) as recorded at page 2197 of Hansard of February 18, 1954, I find he said:
While the port of Vancouver has been working to full capacity . . .
2325
Proposed Committee on Unemployment
This telegram relates to that statement and the unemployment situation. It reads:
Demand immediate reversal of government decision to equalize east-west grain movements. Trade minister Howe misinformed. West coast terminals utilizing only 70 per cent capacity, lack of ships. Loss of trade will result in unemployment. Immediate action imperative.
Grain Workers Union Local 333.
Then, as I indicated, I was away this week end, speaking to the rubber workers in Toronto. They are very worried about the unemployment situation. They see where, right in their own factories, the technological advances of the day are throwing hundreds of them out of work. They indicated to me that their position is very insecure because of collapsing world market conditions, and they fear that any tightening up of the local economy would cause a decline in their local market and aggravate the situation even more.
We do not think we are being unreasonable when we ask this government to make the resources of the unemployment insurance fund available now to ease the situation. After all, by this time the fund has built up to almost a billion dollars. Everyone realizes that in the event of a major catastrophe the fund would disappear; but if there is any way of halting the trend, then the time to use that method is now. We think the workers who own this money have a reasonable request when they ask that the period during which benefits are payable be extended. This is particularly necessary at the present time, when the cost of living is so high.
Much mention has been made of the relationship between unemployment and the high cost of living. There are many who blame high living costs on excessive wage demands. Mr. Speaker, the high cost of living is the result of the deliberate early lifting of price controls. Prices, including wages, began to rise very soon thereafter, and that rise has only recently been halted. We think the high cost of living is due more to an error in judgment on the part of the government's advisers than it is to any rise in wages.
I have noticed also in the debate interjections to the effect that people are unable to find work because of industrial disputes. This business of talking about strikes during this debate is nothing but a red herring. Lost man-hours due to strikes between 1919 and 1953 would not be as great as lost man-hours caused by six months of unemployment.
I agree wholeheartedly with the sound advice given by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) when he emphasized that the government's share in the national economy was a relatively minor one, even though at times the most effective. He pointed out that the government alone was
2326	HOUSE OF
Proposed Committee on Unemployment unable to solve the difficulty, and that it was high time it called in those who are able to wield such an effective influence in the economic life of the country.
I regret that some hon. members representing ridings in which there are large numbers of industrial workers have tried to place the blame for the hungry thirties. I have never been able to blame the Conservative government which was in office between 1930 and 1935 for the conditions of those days. I have *often had the feeling that that government did not take the measures necessary to soften the blow; the blow was felt before it took office. If any government can be blamed-* and I am not sure that it can, because most governments in the world either could not [DOT]or would not know what was coming-that blame would belong to the Liberal government which held office until late in 1930.
To say that in this matter of dealing with unemployment the record of the Liberal government has been the finest in the world is to stretch the imagination to the breaking point. When we see what happened in the United States in the hungry thirties; when we see what happened in some countries of the commonwealth, we see numerous cases where government action was able in large measure to soften the blow and make the hardship less severe on the unemployed.
I am not content to wait to get the facts from some government department concerning this situation. The attitude seems to be to wait until some senior civil servant tells us that we are facing a desperate situation.
I say that the members in this house are in daily communication with the people in their ridings. We ought to know what the situation is, from one end of Canada to the other. We know it is not a happy situation. 1 am not prepared to sit down and wait, or to think that perhaps the warmth of springtime will bring comfort to these people, many of whom, particularly those in the category over 40 years of age, have been without work now for a number of years. May I remind the house that even the President of the United States is not prepared to wait until the warm spring sunshine appears. He has indicated that if these danger signs are still in evidence at the end of next month he will take definite action. I wish we could have the same assurance from the benches of this government.
I know it is felt by some government supporters that the new housing legislation will help relieve the unemployment situation. I think it is timely to point out, however, that it is agreed by the suppliers of building materials, as well as the suppliers of mortgage money, that we cannot expect to see as


many houses built in 1954 as were built in 1953. It is not that the money is not available in the nation, only that it is going to the wrong places. Money at this time should go into the financing of consumer goods, and the building of homes is one such outlet. Because money can make more money elsewhere it is not going into the financing of consumer goods.
I believe there is still plenty of money. I find in this morning's issue of the Globe and Mail an article which reads in part as follows:
Canadian corporations are paying out a total of $28,917,582 in dividends this month, compared with $28,312,571 a year ago and $27,387,006 in February, 1952.
In other words, money available for reinvestment purposes is still being made, and in greater amounts than ever before. However, the main difficulty is, it is not going into the field of consumer goods. There is a great need for an expansion of housing to relieve unemployment, and for other reasons.
The last issue of the British Columbian that I received from New Westminster has a page full of houses of people who are the direct responsibility of the federal government. They are the people who live between the water's edge and the land that is privately owned. I have a lot of that type of land in my riding, and there are hundreds and hundreds of old age pensioners eking out an existence in mere shacks there. Now a British industry is coming along and a causeway is to be built in New Westminster, and many of these old age pensioners are going to be evicted. I would say that the federal government could relieve the unemployment situation by assuring us that they are going to take all these people who are merely existing on federal land in all these municipalities that are on salt water and build decent houses for them.
I should also say, as mentioned, that President Eisenhower is not content to wait until the warm summer sun, and the European nations are not waiting in order to solve their economic difficulties, even if it means doing business with countries behind the iron curtain.
I have often heard it asked, what are your solutions? I think our solutions are well-known, but I should like to remind the government that they have been elected to office and the responsibility for safely guiding the ship of state is theirs and not the opposition's. The responsibility of the opposition is to warn the government, if possible, of the errors that the government may make.
There is a bit of a suspicion in the ranks of labour that to some a certain amount of unemployment may be fine, is looked forward

to, and is even favourably looked upon by those who have to do business with the unions over the bargaining table. I ask this government in all seriousness, is clause 164 of the new Criminal Code the only answer it has to the unemployment situation? It is the section which, if passed, will give the right to arrest all the unemployed of Canada on a vagrancy charge. We ask you in all seriousness to investigate the situation and not to accept the assurance that everything will be all right.
The social needs of the nation are great, and call for an immediate expenditure on public works. We need hospitals; we need highways; we need schools; we need a lot of things. I wonder whether the government, especially the Department of Labour, has considered the possibility of the annual wage. I know there are industries where the annual wage is not practical. However, there are also other industries where the annual wage is a perfectly feasible thing. Where I come from we can build houses the year round, if the building of houses goes forward in an orderly and planned way. I daresay there is not a carpenters' union that would not be prepared to build a house for $500 less, if it could be assured of year-round employment. In our part of the country year-round employment in the house building industry is possible, but it has to be planned. You must have a roof over your head when it rains, or you do not like to work.
Has the government investigated all the possibilities of taking part payment in sterling so that our factories can continue in operation? I wonder whether they fully investigated the possibilities of making more of our goods available to the nations of the world that need those goods. I wonder whether they have investigated the possibilities of increasing the consuming possibilities of the nation.
One of the difficulties of our immigration department, as I see it, is that it has catered to the wishes of those who want to hire cheap labour. I notice, again in this morning's Globe and Mail, an article on a migration plan proposed for homeless United Kingdom children. It is a plan being considered by the government of Great Britain for the emptying of some of their orphanages. In Canada we have a situation not very far from here where up to $3,000 was paid by people who wanted to adopt youngsters. This article says that top government officials at Ottawa are cool in their reactions to the plans that are being formulated in Britain. I can think of no finer way of helping Canada with many of her difficulties, and also in the matter of employment and the sale of our goods, than 83276-1484
Proposed Committee on Unemployment by adding to the small population of Canada. Let us add not only workers to the population; let us let in every orphan in the world who wants to come and live here, and who has an assured home here. We need these people. If we can get them while they are young they will make top-notch citizens later.
The government are not willing to adopt the remedies offered by this section of the house. They are willing to adopt the theory of a planned economy only in time of war, or in some phases of it. I feel that the government is able to do a lot to relieve unemployment, even within the orbit of its own economic thinking.
The great battle of the world today cannot be won with armaments. You must have devoted people to go along with the armaments. Unemployed people and people who are in need are no people to fight a war with. You may have all the armaments you like, but unless the morale of the nation is high you are never going to defeat communism. The fight for peace is worthy of a lot more of sacrifice and a greater effort and devotion than is the battle of war.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we all agree that the matter presently before the house is of grave concern not only to those who presently find themselves unemployed but to every man, woman and child in this country. If things are as black as they are pictured, then we have much to be concerned about. I feel it is regrettable that this debate has been carried on almost to the point of recrimination and in some cases close to slander of individuals and I could say almost equally of groups of people.
The Conservative party without too much recrimination are blaming the Liberals for the weaknesses in our economic system which caused the great depression, while Liberals have been equally vociferous in their declarations that the Conservative party was the cause of the great depression. In the minds of the C.C.F. party we are heading into the same disastrous conditions, while they seek to convince the people that through some magic wand of controls, such as those during the second great war, the present unemployment situation could have been avoided.
2328	HOUSE OF
Proposed Committee on Unemployment
I think these matters might well have been left to the historians. Perhaps the prophets of gloom could be better employed in thinking up some more constructive programs. I have yet to hear any constructive propositions brought forward. Perhaps it is coincidental, but during the speech of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) when, in his usual forceful and if I may say so somewhat indignant manner, he was berating the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) for having made certain remarks regarding a previous prime minister, a page boy brought to my desk a magazine or booklet called Cominco. It is published by the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company for the purpose of giving information to its employees and anyone else who may show an interest in the activities of that company.
There was an article describing the last stages of a $35 million power development on the Pend-d'Oreille river. This power is to be used in the many and varied, and I may say expanding, operations of this company. The power developed at this point will produce enough electricity to light a 60-watt bulb in every home in Canada. It seems to me that is a great concrete example-I may be facetious-of capital investment. It is analogous to the superfluity of words we have heard during this debate, and is a longtime answer in my opinion to the unemployment question.
As I have said, there have been recriminations between political parties, and certain charges have been made. Wishing to be completely fair perhaps I should not say "charges", but there have been inferences drawn on the part of hon. members on this side of the house and, if I recall correctly, by hon. members on the other side, that the labour leaders of Canada are one of the main causes of the present unemployment situation. I think this is most unfortunate as well as being untrue. It is the responsibility of a union leader to see that the workers under his particular jurisdiction maintain an economic balance with every other worker and, for that matter, with the farmers in the Dominion of Canada. I recall that long before I became a member of a trade union my father was a member of a farm organization, a farm union. All these economic units do get together to maintain their proper balance in our economic system.
It has been said that production costs and wages are the reasons for high prices since the end of the second world war. It has been argued, of course, that high prices are the cause of the present unemployment. I think it may be said with equal force that high wages and high prices are perhaps one of


the reasons we have in Canada one of the highest standards of living of any country in the world, so that is hardly a sound argument. We cannot have it both ways.
I think we should look at some of the economic facts that have brought about this situation. It will be recalled that a tremendous productive potential was built up by our factories during the war. Vast sums of money were spent in research and development, which left the country with an internal economy capable of a very high standard. Then what is the cause of high prices? I think we have to remember that almost all non-combatants in Canada during the war made some sacrifice. They bought war savings bonds, they worked harder, and did without some of the amenities of life.
I can remember my own little town, which at the beginning of the war had about 1,200 employees who owned around 800 automobiles. Almost everyone employed was driving an automobile. No new automobiles came into the city during the war, while large numbers were sold to people on farms or people who were in a better position to buy tires and gasoline in the pursuit of their various employments. Undoubtedly it was a small sacrifice when we look back, but we did make sacrifices and because of that there was a vast development.
We were not financing the war entirely by our sacrifices and commitments. Money was created in various ways to the point that after the war there was cash in the banks and securities capable of being converted into cash about three times what there had been before the war. Despite this vast development and stimulus to production, our production did not increase much more than twice. Without some measure of taxation which would have been almost confiscatory, it was inevitable that wages and prices and production would equalize themselves. The labour unions had the inescapable responsibility of maintaining a balance between the wages of employees and the profits of employers. To my mind they have been neither arrogant nor unreasonable.
The hon. member who spoke before me reiterated the C.C.F. claim that the imposition of price controls at this point would have been the answer. I cannot agree with that suggestion. I disagreed with it from the very moment when price controls were removed, and I shall continue to disagree with it so long as I believe in the free enterprise system. I do not believe that was the answer to our problems. Price control could not have meant anything but state control or a further conglomeration of bureaucracy and

interference which would result in lower production. I believe there would have been a considerable amount of bootlegging, black marketing, and so forth.
There is one other aspect of this question which concerns the United States, with whom we have very close economic ties. There we have our greatest market, but they did not see fit at the close of the war to maintain wage and price controls, and if we had clamped on wage and price controls it would also have been necessary to clamp on export controls, because I cannot conceive of a manufacturer manufacturing and selling goods in this country at a price which was pegged, if he could sell to people across the line. Certainly with wages and prices increasing over there the average Joe here would have been left in a very sad state.
There are all kinds of arguments with respect to price controls, but that is one which I believe should be taken into consideration. The underlying and most important objection is that it means statism, and we all know that those countries which have resorted to statism have not yet been able to produce and maintain a standard of living comparable with that enjoyed in this country. That itself should be a sufficient argument.
There is also the question of those who are employed in Canada in industries whose markets enjoy a measure of tariff protection. Some supply the internal market exclusively, and they are perhaps in a more fortunate position. But those who work in industries which depend to a large degree on the export market, and suffer from its fluctuations, are not quite so well off. People in these industries cannot be expected to reduce their standard of living beyond that which is enjoyed by their fellow Canadians. Their standards must be kept in line, and if the export market weakens we have to find ways and means of adjusting the situation.
There is further evidence that it was not wage demands which caused high prices in the base metal and lumber industries. In the metal industry particularly, because of stockpiling by those countries which were preparing for an emergency, prices soared to unheard-of heights. Of course what happened was that the marginal operations came into production. There was high-grading of rich seams, and so forth, until the demand was oversupplied, and naturally the base metal industry is now suffering a depression.
The point I wish to emphasize is that the prices were out of line. I can recall negotiating for a wage increase with the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company at a time when these prices were high. The negotiations were not conducted on the basis of the
Proposed Committee on Unemployment ability of the company to pay. In fact they admitted that prices were high, but claimed they could not pay more despite the fact that they realized there must inevitably be wage demands.
I believe it is commendable that even during this period of high prices some of the large mining companies with great foresight brought in simplified methods of production which improved their over-all efficiency. In co-operation with the unions they doubled their production while using approximately the same labour force. It will be difficult to convince an unemployed miner that this was advisable, but one could point out on the other hand that if this had not been done some of the larger mining companies would be out of business today.
Let us not forget that union leaders, like members of parliament, are elected representatives, and like us they seek only to do a good job. In the same manner as we do, they must face criticism from the members of their unions and be responsible to them for their actions. Like many hon. members of parliament they can always find someone to give them good advice, and there is always someone who feels that given the opportunity he could do the job much better than they are doing it. Union and labour leaders are plagued with advice to desert their present affiliation and join up with some other less militant organization. If they accept that advice they may find to their consternation that their new affiliation has deteriorated greatly in the eyes of the public. In the eyes of many people in Canada, and many employers, the only good union is one which is not asking for something.
Some hon. members have already referred to the rather loose accusations made by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) against some labour union officers, and I must confess that in all the years I have been in the labour unions I have never met any of the individuals described by the hon. member. My reaction to the hon. member's speech might be compared with the feelings of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) when he was rebuking the hon. member for his attack on a former prime minister in regard to the claim that the latter was manipulating the stock market at will.
On February 16 the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Leboe) had this to say as reported at page 2127 of Hansard:
Personally, I am opposed to the professional bargainer. I think it is wrong in principle, because the very existence of the professional bargainer depends on the animosity between the employer and the employee. I will agree that expert advice is desirable. I think we should have
2330	HOUSE OF
Proposed Committee on Unemployment
expert advice, but X believe it is wrong in principle for people to set themselves up in business as professional bargainers-
I might add professional politicians. I suppose there are some, though I have never met them. The quotation continues:
-because their livelihood depends on the animosity between the employer and employee. As soon as good will is created between the employer and the employee the professional bargainer is out of a job.
And further:
I feel that we would be better oil and have a higher level of employment if bargaining were conducted on a local level as much as possible.
I have a few remarks I should like to make with regard to this statement. I am wondering if the hon. member has ever sat in on a session of negotiations with a large corporation represented by their top officials, with the highest legal authority on their side. They are experts in their own fields; for that matter they are specialists. Does the hon. member feel that it is presumptuous on the part of the union to have spokesmen who may have come up from the ranks-and in many cases they have come up from the ranks and gained experience in the process-speak for them? Is this a presumptuous attitude? Or for that matter does he feel that the union takes an unfair advantage by bringing along an adviser trained in research and economics? With regard to this statement, let me say further that a union officer's livelihood does not depend upon perpetuating the class struggle or, in the words of the hon. member, animosity between employer and employee.

Mr. Speaker, I have never had the pleasure of meeting a professional bargainer; that is, apart from union officials. They are union officials who, with their experience, are called upon to go from place to place and assist in the bargaining. The successful labour leader, of whom I think there are quite a large number, is one who mostly knits the labour-management relationships, and who makes economic gains without any strike whatsoever. To be sure, the final decision for action should rest at the local level; that is, with the decision of the rank and file, by their ballots. But the hon. gentleman's plan would result only in a local company union which in effect is no union at all.

I listened with considerable interest to the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), in order to find out whether we had here an answer to the problem. But again there was little light. He sought to prove, perhaps in a different way than I, that wages were not the reason for unemployment today. In his statement he drew to our attention two contracts that had been let in British Columbia.

speechtext:
I am quoting the words of the Acting Prime Minister who was making a statement on what is forecast by way of investment for the coming year. As reported at page 2104 of Hansard he stated:
The survey indicates a capital expenditure program for 1954 of $5-8 billion, roughly 3 per cent above the previous record achieved last year.
Having regard to all the gloom expressed in this house, may I say that I know the matter is serious and that there are many unemployed; but if we let this thing spread too rapidly, it may be possible that some of this investment will not be made. If that investment is made it should mean that there will be a considerable uptrend in the unemployment situation. To continue:
Expenditures for new construction are estimated at $3,865 million, an increase of 6 per cent, while outlays for new machinery and equipment are expected to be 3 per cent lower.
There is still about a 3 per cent increase in the over-all projected capital investment for the coming year.

speechtext:
The increase has been variously stated here, from 3 per cent to 10 per cent; the hon. member can take his choice. I do not think the situation is as bad as some say it is. It is bad; I do not disagree there, but it is not as bad as they picture it.
There are a number of other large developments projected, perhaps not for the immediate future but in the foreseeable future. I think every possible step is being taken to further the St. Lawrence seaway project, not only by this government but the governments of Ontario and the state of New York.
We have the projected trans-Canada pipe line, and we hope there is to be a pipe line from northern Alberta-I would prefer to say southern Alberta and coming through the southern part of British Columbia but I shall stay with the facts, something some members do not do. There is this projected pipe line from the northern part of Alberta down through British Columbia and over to the west coast, which will also supply the Pacific states.
As I have said, these projects are no immediate solution. They do not feed the families of those who are hungry today. The only answer to the immediate problem is perhaps an increase in the unemployment insurance benefits and the extension of those benefits. Why did we institute unemployment insurance if we did not think at some date there was going to be a levelling off, a readjustment of our economy? We have the fund, so let us use it, and let us not be stampeded into a depression.
The estimates before the house contain large expenditures for various projects. I feel we would be well advised to expedite the business of the house so that an early start can be made on these projects. The processing of contracts and so forth requires a considerable time. I suggest that we expedite matters sufficiently to enable these projects to be started by the spring break-up rather than the fall freeze-up. It might be remembered also that under the new arrangements for members' indemnities, the house can adjourn and we can be called together in the early summer without any additional cost to the taxpayers or without any of the formalities required for a normal session. Then we could get down to the business of hammering out a solution to the problem, if that should become necessary.

speechtext:
I
rise to take part in this debate, Mr. Speaker, in the hope that perhaps I may be able to shed some small ray of light on what has seemed to me to be a very confused argument. On one point only does there appear to be complete agreement, a true meeting of minds. Everyone believes unemployment to be a bad thing. Even here there is an element of unrealistic thinking. The Acting Prime Minister has said that even one person unemployed is a serious thing, and the C.C.F. agrees with him. One unemployed person may represent an undesirable circumstance, perhaps even serious from the point of view of the individual concerned, but it hardly represents a serious condition in the nation.
2332	HOUSE OF
Proposed Committee on Unemployment
The C.C.F. introduced a subamendment which is found on page 2096 of Hansard for February 15, 1954 and reads as follows:
. . . the serious and mounting unemployment situation now facing this country calls for immediate action by the federal government to prevent further economic distress.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let us put alongside of that the amendment sponsored by the official opposition and moved by my colleague the member for Vancouver-Quadra, which states that this house is of the opinion that the standing committee on industrial relations should immediately examine into and report upon the actual unemployment situation throughout Canada and present recommendations to this house as to the short-term and long-term methods of dealing effectively with this problem. The C.C.F. subamendment says, in effect, that the unemployment problem calls for immediate action by the federal government. The federal government, however, in the persons of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), the Acting Prime Minister, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), along with the customary echoes, say there is no unemployment problem or if there is it is of such minor proportions as to be inconsequential.
Now, Mr. Speaker, how in the world can you get action on an unemployment problem from a government that says the problem does not exist? The very premise of your argument is denied. Consequently all subsequent argument is a waste of breath. The C.C.F. in supporting their subamendment, where any effort was made to support it, urged the adoption of shopworn socialist solutions which are usually trotted out in cases such as this. Such tinkering with the economy in defiance of economic law is no more likely to be successful here than it has been in other countries. Do the C.C.F. seriously expect, by the sound and fury of their oratory or by the exposition of the socialist dialectic, to convert the government? They cannot possibly be so naive. These oratorical pyrotechnics are designed for public consumption, and in the hope that they may possibly impress unthinking and uncritical people.
In contrast, the amendment of the official opposition is a serious and reasonable attempt to persuade the government to look at the problem and examine the evidence. It recognizes the fact that the government does not believe there is a problem, and reaches the obvious conclusion that as long as the government believes this there is no possible hope of remedial action. The amendment says to the government, in effect, "We do not believe your contention that everything is rosy, but let us take a critical look at all the available evidence. If it shows you are right everybody,


including the Canadian people, will be happy. If it does not show this, you will be advised you are in error, and in addition will possess a body of expert opinion which cannot fail but be of help in devising suitable remedial measures."
Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, I wish to commend in the highest terms the contribution made to this debate by the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden). I thought that in the main he presented a thoughtful and well-reasoned effort. He put his finger on the basic fact in this whole discussion, that employment in this country depends upon the maintenance of export trade. Export trade, in turn, depends upon a price structure that is really competitive. Apart from an occasional irrelevant remark and his somewhat naive and childlike faith in price controls, his speech was a valuable contribution and I should like to compliment him.
Apparently, however, the hon. member does not realize that price controls mean wage controls, and that they extend to wheat and other farm commodities. Moreover, controls as used in wartime were designed to counteract the pressure of scarcity on the price structure, whereas now there is no scarcity but rather an oversupply. Should we embark upon a program of peacetime controls I am afraid it might have consequences far from palatable to the hon. member's constituents- compulsory acreage reduction; dictation as to kind, quantity and variety of crop, to name but a few. This is not a piecemeal proposition. Once you start you have to go all the way.
The hon. member was pleased to use a medical analogy, stressing the fact that you must first diagnose a disease before treating it-a wellnigh perfect argument in support of the amendment put forth by the official opposition. Diagnosis is often a difficult and time-consuming procedure. It requires careful examination of all the available evidence, and in difficult cases the consultation of whatever experts may be available. It is not a haphazard and offhand procedure. The so-called snap diagnosis is the mark of the quack and the charlatan. Could there be a better illustration of the necessity for the objective study of this difficult and complicated subject of unemployment by a committee?
For the foregoing reasons I seriously question whether the C.C.F., in bringing forward their subamendment, are particularly concerned about unemployment, or whether they regard it as a convenient club to belabour the government for fancied political advantage. Bear in mind that only the government can cure unemployment, and they say it does not exist.

I may say I intend to vote for the subamendment, for three reasons; first and most important, because I will have a subsequent opportunity to vote for the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), which really gives some prospect of coming to grips with the problem that, despite what the government says, we in this party believe really exists; and second, because it does say that there is an unemployment problem in this country, something which the government denies; and third, because it is really innocuous and can do no harm.

maintopic: OPPOSITION BY INDIA TO UNITED STATES SUPPLYING ARMS TO PAKISTAN
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-MOTION FOR EXAMINATION BY COMMITTEE ON INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in a country which is adequately equipped with resources and with the means of processing those resources into consumable goods, I think it could be safely said that unemployment is completely unnecessary and is not to be tolerated.
I have listened with considerable interest to speeches from all sides of the house; I think it is pretty well agreed among all hon. members that any degree of unemployment in this country is entirely regrettable and something we all should attempt to remove. Thus far we are all agreed.
The next question is how to do it; what to do to remove this condition of unemployment. It has been suggested that a number of new projects are being contemplated, and that these will provide employment for a large number of men. Whether there will be places for as many men as there are unemployed, or whether those projects will require the kind of men who are now without work, we do not know. We have to take a chance on that. But it is agreed that that is a possible way out of the difficulty.
May I draw to the attention of all concerned something else upon which I think we shall all agree, namely that where there is enough production and productive capacity and resources, we ought to be able to supply everybody in the country with a job. And if we cannot supply him with a job we should be able to provide him with an income, because where a nation is able to produce enough to supply the needs of everybody in the country, then surely it ought to be possible to provide means whereby everybody can obtain his share of the production or at least that share which will keep him living in comfort. I fancy all would agree to that. All would agree that what is physically possible it ought to be possible to make financially possible. If we can produce enough to supply everybody, then it ought to be possible somehow or another to render available the finances with which to enable everybody 83276-149
Proposed Committee on Unemployment to enjoy a fair share of that production. Otherwise we are faced with what looks like foolishness, are we not?
In the days when the Indians owned this country, if they were able to get enough buffalo and enough fish and firewood they were able to live. In our day, if we can produce enough buffalo and enough fish and firewood we ought to be able to live. In order to live we have to have access to an income which will enable us to obtain the share of those goods we need. I believe that up to the present point everyone will agree with what I have said.
Our whole problem is that of rendering financially possible to everyone a good share of the production we can bring into being. There is hardly any doubt that we can produce enough food for everyone in the country, especially enough food to supply the great necessities of life such as wheat, cream, butter and fruit-those things which, taken together, will supply all the real needs of life. We can produce all the shelter required. It is obvious that we can produce all the clothing of the kind required. And so, all down the line, we can produce enough of practically every commodity necessary for life, and physically we can supply everybody in the country with those commodities. If we are not able to do that there must be something wrong with our system of distribution.
Then, since we have begun talking about the system of distribution, there comes to mind the matter of money, because we use money as a means of distribution. If a man cannot obtain access to money he cannot obtain adequate access to goods or services. Consequently the whole matter breaks down to a financial problem, and this is the general approach of the members of the Social Credit movement. We Social Crediters say "Now, if the problem is a financial problem, then let us attack it as such, and see if there is not some way in which we can render financially possible that which is physically possible".
We all admit that what we desire is physically possible, but up to the present time we have not learned how to make it financially possible. Now, how can we make it financially possible? In the last analysis may I repeat to all hon. members and to people throughout the country that the great problem is one of finance, how to create a financial system which will enable the people to enjoy all the goods we can produce.
I do not propose to proceed any further along that line this evening. I think all hon. members will agree with what I have thus far said in this connection.
2334	HOUSE OF
Proposed Committee on Unemployment We have before us in this debate something which, in a way, touched off the debate in the first instance. I refer to the joint submission to the government on February 11 by the Canadian Congress of Labour and the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada. I fancy that since so many have referred to the document in question it might be well for me to give some measure of attention to it.
We find that the drafters of the submission make five main recommendations. I believe one of the great desires in the house, something which concerns members on all sides, is to grant to our labouring people what they feel is their right. Now, are we agreed that what they suggest as being desirable, as a means of attacking this problem, is good?
They advocate first Unemployment Insurance Act amendments. I think we will all agree that these would be desirable. Second, a nation-wide program of public assistance in co-operation with provinces and municipalities; I think everybody in all parties will agree that that would be desirable. Third, a public works assistance program: no specifications are given as to the detailed nature of the program envisaged, but in a general way I think everybody in the house will agree that that also would be desirable. Fourth, a greater encouragement of home building;
I am sure everyone will agree that that is desirable. Fifth, increased aid to underdeveloped countries; and I am sure every member of every party in the house will agree that that recommendation is desirable.
The next question which arises in every mind, I presume, is where are we going to get the money to do all this? So once more the problem works itself out to one of finance.
I do not think there is anyone in the house who doubts that we have the physical capacity in Canada to provide each of those five remedies. We do not say we have not the timber with which to build houses; we do not say we have not the coal to provide warmth; we do not say we lack the physical capacity to do all that is envisaged here, but we do worry about finances; therefore once more we find our problem is primarily one of finances. If we cannot find some way of raising money other than those which we have hitherto used and are now contemplating, then we might just as well give up in despair. That would be the general conclusion.
Inasmuch as our labouring men have not exactly told us where we can get the money, they have not contributed very much to our enlightenment in this all-important aspect. However, I do believe there is a way in which we can find that money.
[Mr. Blackmore.l

Before leaving this submission I would say in a general way that it is highly commendable. We owe a debt of gratitude to the earnest men in charge of our labour congresses who devoted so much attention to the planning and presentation of this submission. I am impressed with two paragraphs near the end of the submission. They are to be found on page 14, as follows:
When unemployment reaches the proportions now being experienced in Canada it has more than economic effects. It carries with it social problems and political potentials which cannot be ignored.
I am sure everyone agrees with that. Then we find this passage:
Unemployed workers and their families must be relieved of their hardship and suffering, but equally important, we must create and maintain a stable Canada, economically, socially and politically.
I am sure everyone will agree with that. Once more the question is, where are we going to get the money to do it? If we can only get the money we can do it. I will say this concerning this submission, before I leave it:	Subject to a reservation or two
because of the need of clarification, in my opinion, of certain phrases in some of these suggestions, I would support the submission wholeheartedly.
There seems to be a disagreement among the people in the house, the government on one side and the opposition on the other, mainly as to whether the unemployment we now have in Canada is of such a serious nature that we need to fear that it indicates the onset of a depression. It is too early for people to tell. It is natural for those who might feel it would be to their political advantage to have a depression, and who would like to blame the government for something very soon, to say this is a serious depression. It is natural for the government to say, "Well, now, it is not quite so serious as you think; at least, we hope it is not". And so we are inclined to disagree to some extent; but facing facts just exactly as they are, I think a good many members on all sides and of all parties think that it is serious enough. I think it is also pretty well agreed on all sides that unless something fundamental is done there will be a serious unemployment problem.
For the last number of years we have been able to keep ourselves employed because we have been fighting a war, or we have been preparing for a war, or we have been indulging in extensive foreign aid programs; mutual aid we have called it, lend-lease we have called it, and various other names. But we are pretty well all agreed that experience has taught us during the last almost 20 years, at least, that we simply must have some means

Proposed Committee on Unemployment
whereby there is a great deal of expenditure on goods that we are not going to use, to consume-such goods and services, we will say, as armaments, training soldiers, dressing soldiers and that sort of thing. We can say this, that sooner or later there will be a depression unless war develops, or there are heavy expenditures in preparation for war, or that extraordinary expenditures for mutual aid or domestic improvements or both come to be a permanent and normal feature of Canada's governmental procedure.
Once more the question arises, where is the money going to come from? Wherever we go we run into that difficulty. Where are we going to get the money? The United States can go on and spend vast sums of money in preparation for war, supporting various nations in their troubles with communism, and all that; but in due time they will reach the limit of their borrowing capacity. They have already reached the limit of their safely taxable capacity. Therefore the question arises, what are they going to do, and what are we going to do when we get into a position similar to that which they have reached?
Without at present going too much into detail as to where we are going to get the money, may I just leave the question tern

porarily and devote attention to this matter of getting money, raising money. We are taxing just as much as we dare tax anybody. We must not go further into debt. We need a great deal more money. Where are we going to get it?
While I am speaking I would suggest that there are some five measures which would give us a good deal of help if we can get the money, and I am sure we can. First is the payment to farmers of a substantial advance per bushel on the grain they store on their farms, provision for adequate storage facilities on the farms, and the payment to farmers for storage of grain stored on their farms.
Those of you who were in the chamber on November 17, 1953, will remember that I outlined a program which I believed would solve the problem of western farmers. I still stand by that program. There have been a good many who found fault with that in one way or another, but sooner or later they have agreed that when I made the suggestions I did on that occasion I was putting my finger right on the essential needs of the situation. I proposed that money should be made available to farmers at not more than 2 per cent, with which to build adequate storage facilities on the farm. That seems so simple that you would believe everyone would say, well, certainly, that is good common sense.
A good many people misunderstood my proposal. They thought I meant that the money would be advanced out of wheat board funds. That is not right. That money should be advanced by the dominion government. Let us consider our Bank of Canada, which was set up in 1934 with a great deal of fanfare. Everybody thought it was going to do wonders for us. Pretty nearly anyone would agree that we ought to be able to get money from the Bank of Canada at 2 per cent to build storage on farms. If the Bank of Canada cannot supply the money we need at 2 per cent to build storage on the farms, then it ought to disestablish itself because it is of little value to us. I think pretty nearly everyone will agree with that.
I advocated that an advance of 75 cents a bushel be made on all grain adequately stored. I believe everybody will agree that that is desirable. I advocated also that there should be a payment of storage on grain stored on the farm, to encourage the farmer to take care of the grain himself and have it on the farm in case of an emergency.
I suggested that Canadian dollars should be advanced to assist prospective buyers of Canadian wheat abroad. I do not think anyone will object to that. We should do that. That principle was applied by the United States, and it worked with great success. They lent money abroad for many years after 1920 with which outside people were able to buy their goods. There is no reason why we should not do the same. It could be done by taking money out of that Bank of Canada. It would be pretty hard to see how anything better could be done with the Bank of Canada.
I suggested also that measures similar to these should be adopted in respect of our coarse grains. If this set of measures alone were adopted all over the three prairie provinces I believe you would find there would be a tremendous loosening up in pretty nearly every aspect of our economy. You would find that those who had sold clothing to the farmers, for example, would be able to get their pay. Merchants would be able to get their pay and would be able to buy clothing and other supplies from Ontario and Quebec which they have been in the habit of buying. To a surprising degree people would be going back into employment, people would begin to buy lumber for houses and all that sort of thing. I venture that you would find probably no measure which would be more immediately beneficial in the matter of restoring employment conditions in Canada than just that set of suggestions which I made on November 17.
2336	HOUSE OF
Proposed Committee on Unemployment
I would suggest as a second means of relieving our problem immediately that we adopt a realistic housing program, one that would make financially possible what is physically possible in the matter of housing in Canada. I am sure it must strike everybody as being simply preposterous that we should have people in this country who are not able to get houses when we have forests of timber in British Columbia all ready to be made into lumber. There are great quantities of lumber in British Columbia just waiting to be brought out to be made into houses. Surely everybody must realize that a preposterous situation now exists.
Once more we come to the matter of finance; and once more I suggest that the financing should be done by the Bank of Canada, which was set up back in 1934. At that time everybody was led to believe that all our financial problems would be solved the minute we got this glorious Bank of Canada. When we got this glorious Bank of Canada it became an impediment to us rather than an assistance in respect of all these vital matters. If the Bank of Canada is not able to do the job then it is time we found out what is the matter. If the Bank of Canada cannot do the job, let us go back to the means we used before we had the Bank of Canada. We had a set-up then which could do this kind of job.
I suggest a realistic housing scheme which would enable people to get money at 2 per cent or even lower in order to build houses, without having to spend $8,000 or $10,000 for a house. Men should be able to build their own houses if they want to, and be able to get the money with which to build those houses without having to comply with a dozen and one regulations that only those with the best kind of incomes are able to comply with.
I suggest as a third measure that we have an extensive and comprehensive reforestation project. We have been wasting our forests up to the present time. I think anyone who contemplates the great forest regions that existed in this country 65 or 70 years ago must feel ashamed because those forests have been wasted in large measure. There are children who will be our descendants in 75 years and who will need forests. What are we doing to provide them with forests? Are we going further to waste this huge heritage that we have, or are we going to rebuild our forests and leave to them fruitful fields for endeavour?
I think everyone agrees that it would be a highly desirable thing if we cultivated our forests. The Germans were able to cultivate their forests to the extent that one hardly saw a stick lying around on the forest floor.


They cared for their forests as though they were gardens. There is no conceivable reason why we should not do the same. By this means we could provide work for many who are now idle. It would not require too great skill to go into the forests and start them growing again. As I have suggested, we need not fear having any unemployed if we embarked on a wide-scale program of reforestation.
People will say, where are you going to get the money? What is that Bank of Canada for? That is what we have to ask. Let us ask ourselves over and over again. When will someone venture to go over to the governor of the Bank of Canada and ask him what they are there for? Ask him what this bank is there for, anyway. Ask him if it was put there as an impediment to Canada or as a benefit to Canada. How can they benefit Canada today except by providing us with money when we need money?

speechtext:
There is somebody down there who is forgetting his responsibility. I am sure that he would not want his constituents to know that that is the kind of thing he is saying in a serious moment like this. Let us just be serious now.
I can remember in 1933 and 1934 when the Bank of Canada was being talked up all over. We were given to understand that it was going to solve our financial problems. Well, it has not begun to do as well as we did under the Finance Act of 1923 and the Finance Act of 1914 in the matter of providing us with money to meet contingencies of this kind. No one has ever taken the trouble to explain why it is not doing that service.
Now, the fourth suggestion I have to make I think was impressed upon us in southern Alberta and in other parts of the country last year particularly, because of the great amount of rain we had there. We should have a comprehensive program of flood and erosion control all across Canada. I hear men rise in this house and talk about how river banks are being worn away by high waters. They talk about the floods that are occurring, that are washing out bridges and all that sort of thing. It is not too soon in this young nation to go to work in real earnest to establish the means of controlling floods.
I know of strategic points all over southern Alberta where control projects could be constructed to stop disastrous floods such as those that struck us in June of last year and which did such tremendous damage. They might have done much more. Similar conditions must exist all over the Dominion of Canada. Why do we not arrange for the controlling of floods like these before too much damage is done? Already enough

damage has been done. If we provided for the controlling of floods all over this country I imagine we would not have very many people unemployed. Of course they would have to be used in the warmer season, but there are things they could do in the wintertime.
I would suggest as a fifth measure that we go right to work in real earnest to build roads all over this country, and do not leave the building of roads entirely to the provinces. Generally speaking the provinces are simply not able to bear the financial burden of building the roads which are necessary. But the dominion can assume that burden if the dominion will use the Bank of Canada, or a Bank of Canada that is modified as it needs to be from what the Bank of Canada now is. I believe that everybody who thinks about this realistically will agree with me.
It is time we had roads all over this country, for many reasons. It is beyond the power of the provinces financially to build those roads. There is only one agency able to supply the finances necessary to build these roads. We certainly have all the means available to build roads. We have the soil that is necessary; we have the rock that is necessary; we can have all the asphalt that is necessary to build these roads. We have people enough to do it. Why not go to work to do it? What is physically possible should become financially possible.
I suggest that by the time we have dealt with these five proposals which I have advanced-they are not original; they have been advanced by various members in the house in this debate-by the time we get done building all these projects, then we can look for other projects. If we cannot find the money, let me repeat once more that the Bank of Canada was established presumably to provide the people of Canada with money. Let those who have the responsibility remember that we are here to find a solution to this problem, not to make silly wisecracks. We were sent here by 15 million people to find the solution, and every single one of us is responsible. Let us bear that in mind, and let us face the problem.
The Finance Act of 1923 and the Finance Act of 1914 provided Canadians with the money to do things. Let us now go on and do things. Let us re-enact the financial measure that can meet the purpose, if the Bank of Canada is too puny to do it. The Finance Act of 1923 was strong enough to do things, and through the strain of world war I the Finance Act of 1914 enabled Canada to do great things. It should be remembered, incidentally, that after the end
Proposed Committee on Unemployment of world war I we had no increases in prices such as we have had at the end of world war II.
That will be enough to start with. 1 leave this contribution for the consideration of hon. members and the country with the promise that at a later date I shall go on with the story.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that in many respects this is the most important debate that has taken place in this house. There has been some disagreement about the extent to which we have unemployment. There has been some disagreement as to the solution for the problem. But I think the important thing to watch is not the figures, which are subject to change from day to day and have often changed for the worse in the past few months, but the trend which has been developing within the past year. That trend is quite noticeable, and I do not believe there is any chance of mistaking it. We are heading back into an unemployment situation. It may recover at times, and at times it may appear to be getting worse, but the general trend is back to the situation which obtained in 1929.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) has moved an amendment, and that amendment calls for immediate action on the part of the government. I regret that it was necessary for the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Trainor), who comes from my own province, to criticize that amendment, particularly from the angle that we might rush into something, and say that in his opinion it was more desirable to set up a committee, or use the committee which existed before, the industrial relations committee, to study this situation and get the facts. I would be rather more impressed with that suggestion were it not for certain historical facts. I have in my hand a publication which appeared in 1934 and which contains quotations from some of the speeches of the then leader of the opposition, Mr. R. B. Bennett.
