speechtext:
No, this goes back to 1930, when he was still leader of the opposition. These speeches were made at various points during the election campaign of 1930. As we know, 1930 was perhaps the beginning of what we call the depression. At that time we already had an unemployment situation in Canada, though it was not as bad as it turned out to be later on. But at that time the leader of the opposition, the late Mr. Bennett, apparently did not believe in setting up committees or holding conferences.
2338	HOUSE OF
Proposed Committee on Unemployment I quote his own words as taken from one of his speeches, made on July 10, 1930, when he said:
The Conservative party is going to find work for all who are willing to work, or perish in the attempt.
Then later on, speaking of the government he said:
Mr. King promises consideration of the problems of unemployment. I promise to end unemployment. Which plan do you like best?
Further on he said:
Mr. King promises you conferences, I promise you action.
That is the kind of language I like. Unfortunately, events proved he was not able to carry out his pledges. I do not wish to lay any particular blame at his doorstep, because the situation did not develop after the Conservative administration took office. It developed before that.
I want to make this quite clear. What we are debating now is not a temporary situation. It is not seasonal unemployment, although there is an element of seasonal unemployment in it. We are debating a problem which has been unsolved in this country since 1929. It is true we have had periods of nearly full employment, but the situation which developed in 1929 and continued until
1939	and well into 1940, under both Conservative and Liberal administrations, was not solved by any government.
One needs only to look over recent pages of history to find that as late as 1938, after three years of a Liberal administration which quite often took credit for having solved the unemployment situation in Canada, there were almost one million people on relief. These are the facts, and any hon. member is at liberty to go back and check them for himself.
It was not until 1940, when world war II came upon us, that the unemployment situation began to disappear. That continued throughout the war. However, let me point this out for the benefit of those who have a habit of sneering at the suggestions we put to the government, and to those who have great faith in private enterprise and its ability to make all things right-and here I am not being critical of private enterprise, but simply stating the facts-that even in
1940	private enterprise was not the motivating force in our economy which solved our problem. The Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Howe) will remember when he, in his capacity as minister of munitions and supply, I believe it was, had to report to this house that with the war already upon us he was not able to place war contracts with a limitation
[Mr. Zaplitny.l

of 5 per cent profit because private industry refused to produce on that limit of profit, and it had to be done away with and they finally received what they wanted.
It was public enterprise by the people of Canada through their war bonds, under the direction of their government it is true, which supplied the war effort, and at the same time as a by-product solved the unemployment problem. During the war when we were devoting half and at times more than half of our total potential to war, and perhaps more than 50 per cent of that was going overseas in war material, the people of Canada lived better, on the average, than they had ever lived before.
That in itself proves that it was not private enterprise, it was not any magic solution by the government, but the fact that for the first time in years the government had used the resources and the power of the nation toward a definite objective which solved the problem. Even when that objective absorbed the best of our population, the best young men most capable of work, and took away more than 50 per cent of the materials that were being produced, the by-product of that effort kept the people of this country on a higher standard of living than they had ever experienced before.
That was the situation when we entered 1945. Again what did we find? When the war ended our so-called prosperity continued. We were quite capable of making outright gifts and extending loans amounting to millions of dollars in the aggregate after the war ended, and despite the fact that we were giving away these things, making these loans, and still using half of our production for purposes other than domestic consumption, we continued to provide the people of Canada with goods and services to a greater extent than they had experienced before the war.
That went on until 1949. By that time great pressure had been exerted upon the government from various sources, some of them in this house, to get rid of wartime controls. There were those who said that we must return as quickly as possible to what they called "normal". I have never been able to find out exactly what they meant by normal. However, they wanted to get rid of all controls and go back to the free enterprise system. Hence by 1949 we began again to have an unemployment situation in this country.
Then came Korea. That is one of the things I find members on the government side do not like to mention very often, namely

the fact that in 1949 we were already beginning to drift back into an unemployment situation. The Korean war did what? It made our national defence budget run into $2 billion and more. Again almost half our potential in this country was devoted to war. Again our economy got a shot in the arm, unemployment began to disappear and things began to move once more. It took a large war and a small one within the last 15 years to burst the financial dams in this country, which had dried up the sources of the medium of exchange, in order to permit us to supply ourselves with the goods and services which have been at our fingertips ever since Canada existed. Those are things we have to recognize. We may agree or disagree upon the solution, but let us at least recognize the facts as they are.
The war in Korea ended, to the relief of millions of people across the world, and we hope that peace will be with us. Now we could turn our attention to the many social problems facing us, and to the improvement and development of this country which is one of the greatest on earth. But what do we find? Instead of entering upon a period of greater prosperity than ever before, and to which every economic and physical factor points, we again find that we are drifting back into what some call recession while others even use that horrible word "depression". Let us call a spade a spade. We are drifting back into a depression; and unless the government are willing to take action they are going to find themselves in the middle of it before they are ready to recognize it or admit it.
We now have-and I am going to use round figures-approximately half a million unemployed. There are those on the government side who say that there are not that many; there are those in the labour ranks who say there are more. But even taking the figures given by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg)-and he stated there were something over 500,000 who had made application for work at the various employment agencies across Canada-and even making some allowance for duplication, if there may be some, it is quite safe to say that there are in the neighbourhood of half a million unemployed in Canada.
This figure represents almost 10 per cent of our Canadian labour force. No one can shrug that fact off or brush it aside by saying it is seasonal unemployment. Now when we are entering the spring season, when that part of the unemployment which is seasonal should be clearing up, what do
Proposed Committee on Unemployment we find? We find that lay-offs are continuing. The unemployment figures are increasing rather than decreasing. That fact in itself proves that the unemployment is not a seasonal matter, and that it is owing to one of the weaknesses in our economic set-up.
There are those who say, "It is all right to talk about giving people jobs, but perhaps there is not enough to do. Perhaps there are just not enough jobs to go around." One has only to travel across the country to see some of the things that need doing. Let me put it this way. In 1953, according to the figures issued by the government itself, our gross national product was in the neighbourhood of $24 billion; in fact it was a little bit over $24 billion. Our population is roughly 15 million. If you do some simple arithmetic you will find that that gross national product comes to a per capita amount of $1,600 for every man, woman and child in our country. Let us take the average family of four; that works out to $6,400 per family.
This means that the nation has already produced or is capable of producing goods and services in order to supply every family in Canada with $6,400 of goods and services if we wanted to use it all in consumer goods. But let us allow one-third of that amount for depreciation and capital expansion; and that figure is one which is considered to be fair. It still means that every family, on the average, in Canada would require an income of over $4,000-about $4,400-to buy back the goods and services which we have already produced.
If we look at the statistics, what do we find? We find that 74 per cent of the wage earners or the people who work in Canada have an income of less than $3,000. We find that 40 per cent of them have an income of less than $2,000. We even find that 14 per cent of them have an income of less than $1,000. How in the world are those people going to buy back the production which they themselves have produced? It stands to reason that there is going to be an apparent surplus.
I say "apparent surplus" because it is not a real surplus. One has only to go through the country-as almost every hon. member does from time to time-go into the cities or the rural areas, to see how many families are living on the bare necessities of life; how many families cannot buy the very simplest luxuries or the very simplest things which make life worth living, apart from food, clothing and shelter; how many are living
2340	HOUSE OF
Proposed Committee on Unemployment in homes which are not fit for human habitation; how many schools have not been painted for the last 50 years; how many hospitals need to be built, and how many first-class roads we could use in this country. Let us think of the hundreds of accidents which occur every year at level crossings across Canada where trains and automobiles collide, and consider the tragedy of it.
Everywhere you turn there is work waiting to be done. Yet we are told by some of our so-called leaders in government, "You just have to get used to the situation; you just have to adjust yourself to the competitive position". Whom are we competing against? This nation is producing $24 billion worth of goods a year and is capable perhaps of producing much more, because we are doing that while we are keeping 500,000 persons idle. If everybody were working our national product would run over the $25 billion mark. Yet we are told that we must get used or adjust ourselves to a competitive position. With whom are we competing? Apparently with ourselves. The goods are there; the services are there. What is lacking is the purchasing power-I refer to the effective purchasing power-in the hands of the people.
The hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) this afternoon was more or less critical of the members of this group for bringing these matters to the attention of the government, the house and the country without putting forward any constructive proposals. That is not an accurate statement, because proposals have been made. But just so that no one will think I am trying to be critical of the government without placing anything before this house, I am going to make some proposals and offer a few comments on at least one of them.
I believe there are five things which the government or this parliament could do and which would be designed to place purchasing power in the hands of the people who could effectively use it. Let me again repeat that it would require an average per family of $4,400 to buy back our production; and that is only that part of the production which can be devoted to consumer goods, after allowing one-third for depreciation and capital expansion. I propose, first, that we should reimpose price controls; second, that we should increase old age pensions, family allowances and war veterans allowances; third, we can reduce the sales tax, which is now 10 per cent, and reimpose the excess profits tax; fourth, that the government proceed with a large-scale public investment program; fifth, reduce interest rates in order to cut the cost of doing business.


I should like to refer briefly to one or two of these points, and I shall start with the question of price control. I have heard a number of members on both sides of the house express themselves as being opposed to price control.

speechtext: Do you accept wage controls too?

maintopic: OPPOSITION BY INDIA TO UNITED STATES SUPPLYING ARMS TO PAKISTAN
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-MOTION FOR EXAMINATION BY COMMITTEE ON INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS
speechtext:
Just possess your soul in patience, and I shall come to that before I am finished. There are those who say they are opposed to controls as a matter of their basic political philosophy. Let us approach it from that angle for a moment. Let us not kid ourselves that we do not have price control in this country today. We did have price control during the war years down to about 1946 or 1947, administered by a board set up by the government. In my opinion that was the most democratic way in which it could be done. There were improvements that could have been made, but at least it was always under the control of the public representatives elected by the people. If there were any grievances or any injustices they could be brought to the attention of the government in this house.
Starting in 1946 the government saw fit to wipe price controls from our statute books. Some people were under the impression when the process was finished around 1949 that we no longer had any price control. Nothing could be further from the truth, Mr. Speaker. We have price controls just as effectively today as we had them in 1945, 1942 or any of those years during the war. The only difference is that price control now has been transferred from the hands of the government to the hands of private industry. No economy, particularly an economy such as ours, could operate without controls. Let no one kid himself that it is possible to do so. It would be no more possible to carry on the economy of this country without some type of control than it would be to drive one of these modem 200 horsepower motor cars without any brakes or steering gear. You would wind up climbing a telephone pole.
Somebody is always going to control the economy of this country. It is for us to decide whether it is going to be the representatives of the people who will set up a system of controls for the benefit of the people, or whether we are going to leave it to private industry to do it for us. They are not going to do it for us; they are going to do it for themselves. They have been doing it very effectively. One has only to glance at the annual reports published by the big companies themselves, and by our financial institutions in recent years, to find that their annual profits are climbing at a great rate.

Proposed Committee on Unemployment
The other day a reference was made to the farm implement industry. One has only to glance at the reports from that industry to find that from 1946 to 1951 their profits increased by approximately 223 per cent. They exercise price control very intelligently for themselves. They are not exercising it for the benefit of all people in Canada; and I, for one, would not expect them to do so. It is not their function. The board of directors of the Bank of Commerce, Canada Packers, Massey-Harris or International Nickel were not set up by the shareholders in order to establish a system of price controls for the benefit of the consumers in Canada. They were put in there to create profits. I want to give them credit for doing a good job. They are making enormous profits. One has only to check their annual reports to ascertain that. You will find that after taxes their profits are still much higher than in any period since 1946, and have been increasing every year.

speechtext: Why not put them on the record?

speechtext:
If I were to put everything on the record to which I made reference I would not get it all into one speech. The hon. member does not need to take my word; he has only to refer to the statistics, and he will find that those profits have been increasing enormously every year since 1946.
The trouble is that while those profits have been increasing, the result of the removal of purchasing power from the people has been dumped, so to speak, in the lap of the government. The government has only the result of the situation but has no control over it. I, for one, have no hesitation in suggesting price control. Let us not get the impression that price control means holding prices down, because in its essence it does not mean anything of the sort. It means bringing about a proper relationship between prices. For example, it is well known today that farmers across Canada are receiving a smaller income for their produce than they have been enjoying in recent years, while at the same time they are paying higher prices for their farm implements, their fuel, their fertilizer and the other things which go into the cost of production.
We are told that trade is one of the ways in which we can keep full employment in Canada. How is a farmer going to produce agricultural products which can sell on world markets at lower prices when his cost of production is going up? Certainly if the government had maintained a sensible system of controls the farmer would be in a position today to produce his products at lower prices, and his price relationship would allow him
to sell his goods on the markets of the world. His standard of living would not be impaired.
A question was asked a while ago as to whether or not I was in favour of wage controls. Let me tell my hon. friend that what I said a moment ago about industry taking over price control holds true for labour. Industry is doing a job in controlling wages. Ask any labour union about that, and they will give you the full story about wage control. What we need is control of prices which are being manipulated by monopolies and combines at an international level.
Again let me say it is not the business of private industry to maintain a proper price level; that is not their function. Their function is to produce goods and make a profit.
I have no criticism of the fact that they are making huge profits. It is the function of this parliament to watch and protect the welfare of the consumer in this country, particularly the welfare of those senior citizens of ours and the veterans who are on fixed incomes or pensions. They are the first to be hurt when the cost of living begins to spiral.
I want to refer also to the question of public investment. From time to time, in fact since 1945 when the famous green book proposals were put out-the government has been putting out so many of these books we get our colours mixed, but I believe it was the green book proposals-we have been told that it was the intention of this government to launch upon a wide scheme of public investment by way of necessary public works, and also to initiate certain industries where necessary. The years have gone by since 1945, and nothing has come out of it. In recent months announcements have appeared in the press to the effect that the government has some sort of plan, "built-in stabilizers" as they call them, and certain fiscal policies which would prevent a recession.
I think it is time these mysterious hat tricks of the government were brought to light. Let us see what these built-in stabilizers are. Let us see where their public investment program is. For what reason are they holding back? We were told, in 1946 I believe it was, that the government had a shelf of public works that was being held for just such an emergency as this. So far as I can see it is still on the shelf. It has not been brought before this parliament. It has not been brought to the attention of the country, and the situation is becoming worse each day.
We say, Mr. Speaker, that there is an immediate problem. I hope something can be done immediately now that the problem is
2342	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Proposed Committee on Unemployment here. At the same time let us not kid ourselves into thinking that within a few months we are not going to have an unemployment situation, and that we can just sit back and wait until next year, or until the problem reappears. It will not work out that way. The purchasing power of the people is being drained off in the form of profits at a greater rate today than ever in the history of Canada. If that process continues, and if there is nothing in the form of government policy to replace that purchasing power in the hands of the people who need it and who will use it, then our unemployment problem will increase and snowball until we reach a major depression within a very short time.

maintopic: OPPOSITION BY INDIA TO UNITED STATES SUPPLYING ARMS TO PAKISTAN
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-MOTION FOR EXAMINATION BY COMMITTEE ON INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, now that parliament has increased my yearly remuneration by some $4,000-and, I might add, without my consent-I for one intend to do my very best to try to earn that extra money. Perhaps that is a challenge to some other members who may wish to do likewise. I would warn them, however, that if no effort is made to place themselves in the position of $10,000 a year men, many of them will never get past the next general election, and will not be here to enjoy that remuneration.
I had not intended taking part in the debate because, as hon. members know, we are getting on toward the end of it. However, no one has mentioned the point I intend to discuss at this time, and that is my reason for rising. If someone had said these few words I intend to say I would not have bothered getting to my feet.
The government most certainly must accept a share of responsibility for the unemployment situation as it exists today. The government, and in particular the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris), are responsible to a greater extent than they care to admit. Hundreds of thousands of immigrants were brought to this country as agriculturists, their contracts stating that they were to stay on the farms for a period of one year. What happened? Many of them left their employment in one or two weeks, leaving farmers high and dry, and migrated to the towns or cities to find employment, perhaps to be absorbed in industry.
I remember warning the minister about three years ago that the immigration laws should be changed, extending the time to about five years. This would have stopped many of the immigrants coming here as agriculturists. They found the only way they could get into Canada was to come as agriculturists, and we know that many of them were not qualified for that work when they came here and had no intention of remaining on the farms. If they had been told that they 
would be kept on the farms for a longer period of time they would not have come out in the first place. This, to my mind, would have done more than anything else to assure jobs for thousands of men, because it would have stopped many others from coming to Canada in the first place.
Their only way to get into Canada was to come here as agriculturists, and I say the government should have compelled those men to fulfil their contracts. The second mistake was made when the government refused to accept advice to change the provision in the immigration law from one year to a period of from three to five years. This would not have been any hardship for those who intended to make agriculture their life's work, and I am sure it would have had the result that many who now are unemployed would have been working steadily.
There are many farms in this country that could absorb more men than are now available. In addition to this, many farmers cannot afford to match the prices offered in industry. That is one reason men have left the farms; they can get higher wages elsewhere. But had they been compelled to fulfil their contracts when they were brought out here in the first instance we would have found that a great many men who are now walking the streets would have been on those farms and doing good work. However, as these men were probably the last to be absorbed into industry, they have been the first to be let out. That is one of the reasons why unemployment figures run so high at the present time.
To work is not a hardship-that is, unless there is something else one would rather do. One reason there are so many out of work in the farm machinery plants is that the farmers have stopped buying farm machinery. The machine companies have priced themselves out of the market, and the farmer cannot afford to pay farm machinery prices. Labour costs are too high. How can we expect anything but unemployment when the farm income has dropped by about 30 per cent? If the government wants to lessen the degree of unemployment all it has to do is to step up farm prices, and just watch the unemployment situation disappear.
Another factor that is unfair to the farmer is the income tax. Working hours should be considered when farm income is being computed. Why should farmers pay the same rate of tax on income earned when it requires twice as many hours to acquire the same amount of money? And we know, too, that farming is always a risk. The farmer never knows, after having worked to prepare

land for a crop, whether he will receive a suitable return, because much depends on the weatherman.
In closing let me say that the government must accept responsibility for at least a third of the number of unemployed, by reason of not having done those ordinary things one would expect it to do to assist the workingman. Export markets as we know are not very encouraging, and the world demand for wheat has been less buoyant. Continued surplus production in the United States does not brighten the hopes for Canadian producers. Cattle prices have dropped by at least a half in the last two years.
Then federal taxation has done as much as any other single thing to create unemployment. If taxes were to go down the cost of living would go down, as well as the cost of production. We should then find ourselves in a better position to compete for world markets. I most certainly hope the government will consider these problems.

speechtext:
No, not for the
government. Looking over the debates of the House of Commons of about 20 years ago, I came across precisely the same sort of debate we are having today, on the subject of unemployment, by way of an amendment to the motion to go into supply. I find that almost the same kind of thing was being said then as we have heard today.
For instance, at page 1275 of Hansard for April 4, 1930, I find a speech by my old friend Henry Spencer, in which he speaks of the unemployment situation and points out that at that time the number of unemployed in Canada stood, in round figures, at 100,000. That interested me, because at that time it was quite obvious that members of the house on all sides were taking the unemployment situation extremely seriously. Yet here we had a figure of 100,000 out of an admittedly lower population of about 10 million. That is, there was only a fifth of the number of
Proposed Committee on Unemployment unemployed we have today, at a time when the population was two-thirds of today's population.
Now, of course not all people at that time took the same serious view of the matter that Mr. Henry Spencer did. We had another gentleman who was, need I say, a government supporter of the day, a member of the Liberal party in 1930, and he had this to say in part, as reported at page 1347 of Hansard for April 7, 1930:
During the summer season of 1929 this country enjoyed the greatest era of prosperity that it had known since confederation. Never in the history of this nation have we enjoyed greater prosperity, greater development and greater contentment, and nowhere else in the world could a labouring class be found who enjoyed a higher standard of living than did the people of Canada during the year 1929.
Mr. Speaker, one might almost have imagined that the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Howe) was speaking. Yes; and then, as my Conservative friend says, "came the deluge". But the deluge was in the form of a Conservative government, which arrived in 1930. In Hansard for 1931 we have the report of speeches made at that time, in which the prime minister of the day is quoted as having said this, as reported at page 465:
I tell you that when parliament meets, if there is not then evident further increase in employment, additional steps will be taken to meet the situation.
And the hon. member who quoted him said this:
I believe, Mr. Speaker, we have a right to know what those additional steps are to be.
Again that is curiously reminiscent. I refer you, Mr. Speaker, to a more recent Hansard, as recent as February 12 of this year. At page 2026 we find a statement by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) in answer to a question regarding the fiscal and monetary measures which, according to the Acting Prime Minister, this government is now implementing to prevent a rise in the level of unemployment. I find in it very much the same sort of vague assurance that the people of Canada were receiving from their spokesmen in 1930 and 1931.
I suggest that it is time the government began to take a little serious interest in the actual state of affairs in Canada, that they should take their heads out of the sand, that they should, for instance, perhaps listen to the voice of the executive commission of the Canadian association of social workers whose corresponding secretary had a letter in the Toronto Globe and Mail this morning, from which I should like to quote a few rather striking sentences:
Last year, after most careful study by the Canadian Welfare Council and its membership across
2344	HOUSE OF
Proposed Committee on Unemployment
Canada, representations were made to the government at Ottawa and to all provincial governments regarding the urgent necessity of having some over-all and permanent provision made to meet the situation and avoid the destitution and disruption of normal family living which today faces many families through no fault of their own. As far as can be observed, nothing has been done to make effective the recommendations made in this report or to evolve any satisfactory alternatives. Unemployment of able-bodied employable people who need and want work is a national problem which strikes at the very roots of family life and causes untold suffering.
There is more in the same vein, Mr. Speaker, which indicates that people whose daily work brings them into close contact with the unemployed are viewing the situation today with a great deal more gravity than our spokesmen on the government benches are doing.
It may be that such champions of free enterprise as the government of Canada will pay more attention to such sturdy enterprises as Messrs. Dun and Bradstreet rather than to the presumably soft-hearted and sentimental social workers. Messrs. Dun and Bradstreet have some rather shattering information for us too, as published in the Financial Post of February 13 of this year, where they report the number of business failures in the years 1952 and 1953. They tell us that in 1952 we had 843 business failures; in 1953, 1,039, an increase of 23 per cent. But worse than that, the number of business failures in the last quarter of 1952 were 192. In the last quarter of 1953 there were 317 failures, an increase of 65 per cent.

The liabilities of those failing concerns presented an even more serious picture. In 1952 the total liabilities of business failures amounted to $21,823,000. In 1953 the liabilities amounted to $30,704,000, an increase of 40 per cent. But here again we find that the final quarters of each year present an even more depressing picture. In the last quarter of 1952 the liabilities of business failures amounted to $4,605,000; whereas in the last quarter of 1953 the liabilities amounted to $10,325,000, an increase of 125 per cent.
Since it is ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I beg leave to move the adjournment of the debate.
On motion of Mr. Cameron (Nanaimo) the debate was adjourned.
